# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead

*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*

---

## 0. How to use this document

This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.

**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**

- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.

**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**

1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 16 makes that jump concrete.
3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.

---

## 1. The one principle everything hangs on

> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**

Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.

Two corollaries the training hammered:

- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.

Everything else is mechanics in service of this.

---

## 2. The dual mandate

You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:

- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.

Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:

| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
|---|---|---|
| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |

The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.

---

## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff

The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:

- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.

**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.

**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.

- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.

---

## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on

**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.

You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:

1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*

**Set a persistent baseline at the account level.** Account instructions change Claude's default behaviour across *every* conversation. The working style this session describes — "lead with the point, flag the trade-off mid-response, challenge like a senior reviewing a PR" — is the target. What you actually have today is a *tool-configuration* baseline, not a committed instructions file: a global effort dial and a curated plugin list that already push back on rubber-stamping (see §16.2). That's a real approximation, but don't assume the gap is already closed — closing it deliberately means writing the actual instructions, not just configuring the tool around the edges.

- *IC discipline:* Never accept the first response on anything that matters. If Claude found nothing wrong with your plan, that's a signal to apply technique 1 or 2, not a signal you're done.
- *Lead discipline:* Make anti-agreeableness a *team norm*, not your private trick. A squad that accepts Claude's first answer wholesale will produce a codebase full of unexamined assumptions. Teach the four techniques. Put them in the shared rules. Ask in regroup: *"What did Claude agree with that it shouldn't have?"*

---

## 5. Context and thread hygiene

Long conversations degrade output. Every message carries the full history; on a long thread the relevant signal gets buried in noise and quality quietly drops.

The rules:

- **New conversation when the topic shifts.** Topics bleed across context and pollute each other.
- **Name conversations like files, not chat logs.** `checkout-fetch-pattern`, not "SFCC stuff." Treat them as a structured archive you can navigate.
- **Aim for 8–10 named, focused threads**, not one 80-message thread called "Zimmermann."
- **Claude.ai Projects share context across conversations** — use a Project for planning. **Claude Code uses the repo's rules/context files instead** (`CLAUDE.md` + the `.claude/` layer).

- *IC discipline:* One topic per thread. The moment you notice yourself pasting unrelated context to "remind" Claude, you needed a new thread three messages ago.
- *Lead discipline:* At team scale, thread hygiene stops being about *your* signal and becomes about *shared* context. What lives in a personal thread is invisible to the squad; what needs to be shared belongs in the Project or the rules layer, not buried in someone's chat history. Decide, as lead, what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact — and make that call explicit so the team isn't guessing.

---

## 6. The planning layer — your codebase's constitution

This is where the quality ceiling is actually set. In the training it was a `.claude/` structure; on your project it's the equivalent rules-and-context layer (section 16 maps the names).

### `CLAUDE.md` is a contract, not a readme

It tells Claude exactly **what to build**, **how to build it**, and **what NOT to do**. Claude Code reads it at the start of *every* session. It is the entry point every prompt begins from.

- **Use Claude to *critique* the contract, not rewrite it.** Ask what's wrong; fix one problem at a time. If you let Claude rewrite it wholesale you get a file that reflects Claude's assumptions, not your decisions.
- **Each fix should change *structure or specificity*, not wording.** Polishing sentences is procrastination. If your edit didn't change what Claude can or can't do, it wasn't a real edit.

### One topic per file — a hard rule

If a file covers two things, Claude gets confused about which one applies. So: `build-spec.md`, `solution-architecture.md`, `auth-spec.md`, `design-system.md`, `api-patterns.md`, `component-registry.md` — one concern each. The training's own structure split a `brief/` folder (the *what* and *how*) from a `rules/` layer (the enforceable constraints Claude checks against).

**Monolith vs split is a real decision.** Both are defensible *if you can defend it* — but the split is where a serious project lands. A monolithic file and a split set of files produce genuinely *different* Claude Code output. Know why you chose yours.

### `build-log.md` is memory, not documentation

Claude reads it at the start of every session to know what state the project is in and what's already been done. It is how a fresh Claude Code session — with no memory of yesterday — picks up where you left off.

### Define "done" — or Claude Code never stops

Claude Code with no stopping condition keeps building components forever. If your file doesn't say what "done" looks like, Claude will invent more work. **Where does your file say what done is?** If it doesn't, that's a bug in the plan, not the tool.

- *IC discipline:* Before you build, three questions must be *yes*: does Claude know exactly what to build, exactly how, and exactly what not to do? If any is no, fix it before you open Claude Code.
- *Lead discipline:* The planning layer is the highest-leverage thing you own. **This is a system, not a personal note.** A rule that isn't checkable is an aspiration Claude will ignore — police the difference across the whole `rules/` layer. And because two squads read the same files, ambiguity here isn't one dev's rework, it's a fork in the codebase. Owning this well is worth more than any component you'll personally write.

---

## 7. Gap-hunting before the build

**Find every gap before Claude Code does. Every gap in your planning files costs time in the build** — and on a fixed-price job, that time comes out of margin.

**Use two reviewers with different mindsets, in order:**

1. **Claude.ai first** — the conversational reviewer. Prompt it as a senior engineer handing the project to a junior who'll build it with Claude Code: *"Find every place Claude Code would have to make an assumption because I haven't told it what to do. Be specific. Don't be kind."*
2. **Claude Code second** — the builder's reviewer. *"Read all files. Do not write code yet. Tell me: every assumption you'd have to make; every instruction that conflicts with another; every topic the files don't cover; check framework versions are current LTS; check the sample code is correct and uses our methodology; any flaws with downstream impact. Reference the file and line for each."*

**The contrast between what Claude.ai flags and what Claude Code flags is the lesson.** Claude.ai catches conceptual holes; Claude Code catches build-breaking ones. Whatever gaps remain after both — they're *knowable*, and knowable gaps are the ones you can close.

**The distinction that separates real work from theatre:** *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* Acknowledging a gap in conversation and moving on is the seductive failure. Fixing means the file changed.

- *IC discipline:* Run both reviewers on your own stories before you build. "What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?" is the most useful question you'll ask all day.
- *Lead discipline:* Institutionalize the two-reviewer pass as a squad ritual before any sprint. And guard against acknowledge-don't-fix at the team level — in review, don't ask "did Claude flag anything?", ask "show me the file line you changed."

---

## 8. Scaffolding discipline

**Do not scaffold by hand.** Running the framework's project generator manually (`create-next-app` in training; the PWA Kit generator on your project) *skips the brief entirely* — Claude Code won't wire up your design tokens, routes, env vars, or folder structure, and you'll spend Wednesday paying for it.

Instead: let Claude Code **read the brief and execute every setup step**, as an explicit numbered sequence — configure design tokens, set up fonts, create the folder structure from the architecture file, wire env placeholders, create the build-log with a setup checklist as its first entry. **Confirm each step; list every file created at the end.**

- *IC discipline:* After generation, don't trust — verify. Open the token config; missing tokens cause compile errors downstream. A green scaffold checklist exists precisely so this moment is fast and unambiguous.
- *Lead discipline:* The scaffold sets conventions the whole squad inherits. Get the folder structure, token config, and env contract right *once*, centrally — every shortcut here is multiplied across every developer who builds on top of it.

## 9. The build loop — the core craft

This is the part that "makes the methodology different from just prompting." Everything above exists to make this loop clean.

### 9.1 Atomic design, bottom-up

Build in layers: **layout primitives → atoms → molecules → components.** The lower layers are the foundation; you generate them from the design-system spec *first*, review them carefully, and everything above imports them.

### 9.2 The story skill — consistency at scale

A **skill is a reusable Claude prompt** that produces consistent, buildable output given a component name. You build one `story-skill` conversation and drive it with a command: `/create-story [ComponentName]`.

A good story is **thin — intent and constraints, not implementation detail.** The non-negotiable format:

- Follows the story template exactly.
- References the *correct* design file and the *correct* data stub (or none, for static components).
- **AC describes behaviour, not implementation** — something a tester can verify without asking a developer what it means.
- **Always includes happy path + loading-state AC + error-state AC.** Three states, every time.
- **Flags anything uncertain rather than inventing it.**

**The skill is only as good as its prompt — and the prompt gets better every time you find a gap in its output.** Run it, find what it invented or left vague, refine one thing, run again. The second output is tighter. *That iteration is the lesson* — it's the same feedback loop as section 9.6, applied to your tooling.

### 9.3 Generate is 10%. Review is 90%.

Generating a component or a story takes a minute. **The work is the review.** A bad story generates a bad component; five minutes reviewing a story now saves an hour tonight.

**Hard rule: no one builds from a story they haven't personally read and checked.** Not you, not anyone on the squad.

### 9.4 The registry — import, don't reinvent

`component-registry.md` lists what exists, where it lives, and its data source. Before building anything: **check the registry and import what's there — do not rebuild atoms inline.** After building: **update the registry.**

The test: *"If Claude Code opens this repo tomorrow with no memory of today, does it find a registry that tells it what's already built?"* On a solo project that's a convenience. **On two squads it's the difference between reuse and three developers building three different `StatusBadge`s.**

### 9.5 The loop itself

> **story → build → review → correct → commit.** One story, one prompt, one review, one commit.

The build prompt pattern, every component: *read the registry, read the design-system rules, read this component's story, read the design file — confirm what you read before writing a single line of code — build exactly as specified, import from the registry, don't reinvent.*

- *IC discipline:* Run the loop honestly on your own components. When Claude Code does something the story didn't specify, that's a defect in the story — go fix the story (9.6), don't just patch the code.
- *Lead discipline:* The loop is what you're teaching and enforcing. In review, verify the loop *ran*: "Did Claude Code read the story before building, or did you just hand it the design file?" A squad that skips the story and prompts from the design file is doing exactly the thing the methodology exists to prevent.

### 9.6 The feedback loop that hardens the rules layer

The most important habit for long-term quality:

> **"Find one place where Claude Code made a decision you didn't specify. What would you add to the AC or the rules to prevent that next time?"**

Every correction is data. A correction you make once and forget is a correction you'll make fifty times across the codebase. A correction you *push back into the story template or the rules layer* is made once, forever, for the whole squad. This is how the rules layer becomes real instead of aspirational — and it's pure Lead leverage.

## 10. The quality bar and the anti-patterns

### The hardening checklist — every component, non-negotiable

Run this on every component before it's "done." (Stack names are translated to your project; the *intent* is verbatim from training.)

- **Mobile layout at 375px** — actually open dev tools and check.
- **Loading state present — a skeleton, not a spinner.**
- **Error state present — a proper error component *with retry*.**
- **No hardcoded hex values — design tokens only.**
- **No TypeScript `any`** — strict mode on. *(This is already your default per your working style — hold the squad to it.)*
- **Deployed and resolving — matches local, not just running locally.**
- **Registry updated with everything built.**

### Anti-patterns to catch on sight

- **Over-engineering.** A static banner that should be ~25–35 lines of JSX comes back as 120 — that's Claude over-engineering; simplify it. If a trivial component takes too long to build, the problem is usually the atom layer underneath, not the component.
- **Logic in the wrong place.** Derive calculated values (a `percentUsed`, a `daysRemaining`) **in the component, not the hook** — or wherever your `api-patterns` rule specifies. The point isn't the specific rule; it's *consistency* — watch for Claude Code *drifting* from the pattern across components.
- **Fetch inside the component.** Data-fetching follows the shared pattern (a hook / service layer), *not* inline in the component.
- **UI state vs server state confusion.** A local toggle is local UI state — it does not round-trip to the API. Know which is which and don't let Claude blur them.
- **Invented data sources.** A *derived* component (one whose data comes from other components' data) does not get its own stub or its own API call. If Claude invents one, **fix the story, not the code.**
- **Rebuilt assets.** Complex SVGs / illustrations get copied from the design file verbatim — don't let Claude "recreate" them from scratch.
- **Hardcoded-per-item logic.** Icon or variant selection driven by a `type` enum, not a hardcoded branch per item.

- *IC discipline:* Harden your own work to this bar before you'd dream of asking anyone else to.
- *Lead discipline:* This checklist is your review rubric and your definition of team-done. The over-engineering and drift checks especially are things *only a senior eye catches* — juniors accept whatever compiles. That catch is a large part of what you're paid for.

## 11. Shipping discipline — pragmatism under a fixed-price clock

The training's pragmatism is directly relevant to a fixed-price, deadline-bound delivery:

- **Deploy first.** A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible — to the review, to the client, to everyone. *"A local build that hasn't shipped is invisible to the regroup."*
- **A partial-but-hardened deliverable beats a complete-but-broken one.** *"A deployed page with a loading state beats a perfect local component."* *"A partial portal with hardened components beats a complete portal with broken states."*
- **Descope — never cut.** When something runs over: reduce scope (the complex chart becomes a data table — same data, no charting library), commit a loading-skeleton placeholder, and move on. **Never delete the component entirely.** Something honest in place beats a hole.
- **The 20-minute rule.** If a fix will take more than ~20 minutes right before a deadline, it's not worth doing before the milestone. Ship what's done and done well; log the rest.
- **Compare against the design, side by side.** Design file on one half of the screen, live URL on the other. Divergence you can't see, you can't fix.

- *IC discipline:* Make the descope call on your own work early and without ego. Running over at the 80% mark? Stop, commit a clean placeholder, move on.
- *Lead discipline:* You own the *triage* across the squad — what gets hardened, what gets descoped, what gets cut for the milestone. Protecting the quality bar under deadline pressure is the specific test of whether you're actually leading or just hoping. Hold the bar when it's inconvenient; that's when it counts.

## 12. Cross-cutting dimensions — the "etc."

The user asked for the *etc.* explicitly. Here is the full dual-lens reference — the same eleven capabilities, each in both hats. This is the section to reread before a hard week.

**Think.**
IC — one component deep: states, edges, and *what Claude will get wrong before it does.* Lead — one system wide: does this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, the go-live sequence, maintainability in 2027?

**Ask.** *(full question bank in section 13)*
IC — the questions that expose gaps in *a story*. Lead — the questions that expose gaps in *the rules layer, the conventions, and the team's understanding.*

**Communicate.**
IC — precise AC, precise commits, precise "here's what Claude got right and what I corrected and why" (specificity over politeness — the *correction* is the more valuable half). Flag uncertainty; never invent. Lead — frame reviews as *work-not-person*; translate across dev/BA/tester/SA; keep the showcase *honest, not polished*; make every commitment specific enough that someone could check it in three months.

**Decide.**
IC — monolith-or-split for *your* files, hook-or-component for *this* value — and be able to defend it. Lead — set the *convention* so the squad doesn't re-litigate the same decision every component; document it in the rules layer.

**Review.**
IC — your own output against the story, before commit, honestly. Lead — run the loop that makes *everyone's* work legible; catch pattern-drift across the codebase that no single-component view reveals.

**Ship.**
IC — deploy your own work, descope early, no ego. Lead — triage what hardens / descopes / cuts across the whole squad against the milestone.

**Improve.**
IC — every correction you make, push back into your story or prompt so you never make it twice. Lead — push corrections into the *shared* rules layer so the *squad* never makes them again. This is your highest-leverage move.

**Protect quality.**
IC — your commit is clean (no `any`, no hex, three states). Lead — the bar holds across the codebase *under deadline pressure*, including when holding it is inconvenient.

**Manage context.**
IC — one topic per thread; named threads; short threads. Lead — decide what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact and make it explicit, so team knowledge lives in the Project and rules layer, not in someone's chat history.

**Handle uncertainty.**
IC — flag what you (or Claude) are unsure of rather than inventing; distinguish "verified" from "assumed." *(This is already how you work — it's your verification mindset. Keep it.)* Lead — make "flag, don't invent" a team norm; keep an open-items list visible; never let an assumption harden into a fact silently.

**Multiply / mentor.**
IC — you get faster and cleaner. Lead — *the room* gets faster and cleaner because of how you work. You are the capability anchor; knowledge you don't transfer is a single point of failure wearing your name.

**Think beyond.**
IC — the next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. Lead — what happens when you're *not in the room*: the team you're growing, the second squad's dependencies, the integration seams, the go-live risk, the two-year maintainability of every convention you set.

### Questions you ask the squad / the codebase (Lead hat)

## 14. Rituals to run — review culture as delivery practice

The training's *regroup* is your review culture. On the project you're the facilitator, under real stakes. Run it deliberately:

- **Every work block gets a regroup.** Build, then look at real work together. The regroup exists *to learn from the work, not to judge the person who wrote it* — say that out loud and mean it. This norm is the whole thing; without it people hide their work and you lose visibility.
- **Rotate who's on screen.** Don't only review the confident volunteers — deliberately surface work from people who haven't been seen. (The training literally cold-picks, and bribes volunteers with snacks. Do the humane version: make it safe, make it normal, make it everyone.)
- **Ask structural questions, not surface ones.** "Is this well-written?" is the wrong question. "What will Claude *do* with this?" is the right one. Push people from fixing words to fixing structure.
- **Rolling verbal reviews, not just projector sessions.** One person shares one surprising flag; the room reacts. Cheap, frequent, low-ceremony.
- **The showcase is honest, not polished.** When you demo up or across, show what was *built*, not what you were *trying* to build. The single most valuable thing to surface is *"one thing the AI got right that followed from our rules, and one thing we corrected and why"* — the correction is the more important half. Model this; it sets the honesty bar for the squad.
- **Commitments are specific enough to check.** "Use Claude more" is not a commitment. *"Write the AC before I open Claude Code, not after"* is. Hold yourself and the squad to actionable specificity — the kind someone could verify in three months.

## 15. How you'll know you're slipping

Failure signals, by hat. If you catch these in yourself, correct before they compound.

**IC drift:**
- You accept Claude's first response on things that matter.
- You're editing wording in your planning files instead of structure.
- You built a component without reading its story, or without checking the registry.
- You corrected Claude and moved on without fixing the story.
- You have one 60-message thread called "Zimmermann."

**Lead drift:**
- You haven't touched the codebase in weeks — your reviews are becoming vibes.
- Your rules layer has aspirations in it that Claude Code demonstrably ignores.
- You're fixing the same Claude mistake in five components instead of fixing it once in the rules.
- Reviews feel like judging people, and people have started hiding their work.
- You're the only one who knows how a convention works — you haven't transferred it.
- Under deadline you quietly dropped the quality bar and didn't say so.

- All three carry a `Status — done. Kept for traceability.` banner.
- Each one lists doc-artifact paths under a bare `docs/` directory as part of what it produced — and that directory doesn't exist anywhere in this repo. (The code/config artifacts they describe — `digital-sit.yml`, `playwright.config.js`, `.browserstack.yml`, and others — are all real and verified; only the documentation half of the "done" claim is stale, likely left behind by the project's later move to Confluence.)
- This is the literal version of §7's own question: *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* These files acknowledged a plan and marked themselves done. Nobody went back to check.

**4. Does `/code-quality`'s own default command even run?**
- Its `SKILL.md` says: if no argument is given, run `git diff --name-only main`.
- Run that in this repo today and git errors immediately — `fatal: ambiguous argument 'main': unknown revision or path not in the working tree` — there is no local `main` branch, only `develop`.
- Even where `main` resolves (say, after a fetch), it's the wrong base per `AGENTS.md`'s own Branch Rules table: `feature/*` and `fix/*` branch from `develop`, so diffing against `main` would pull in everything already merged to `develop` from unrelated, already-finished work.
- `/pr-checklist`, which calls `/code-quality` internally, gets this right — it diffs against `develop`. The two skills disagree with each other, and the one most people would reach for on its own is the one that's broken.

All four are the "is this a rule Claude can check against, or an aspiration it will ignore" failure mode from §6 — except worse, because each would pass a casual read. #1 would route a PR to the wrong reviewer, or actively misinform a new hire on day one. #2 means two Claude Code sessions on this same repo could legitimately behave differently depending on which rule they happened to read first. #3 means a document you'd otherwise trust as "done" is quietly missing half of what it claims. #4 means the tool you'd reach for to check your own work fails outright unless you already know to pass it an argument. Acknowledging all four in this paragraph isn't the fix, per §7's own distinction — the fix is whichever file actually changes.

### 16.5 The honest close

The training gave you a *transferable methodology* and proved it on a solo React build. Your job takes that methodology into **shared-codebase, two-squad, fixed-price delivery on a stack you don't yet have deep muscle memory in.** The discipline carries over completely. The framework fluency and the leadership craft are the two things you have to build deliberately on top of it.

What's different now versus when this section was first written: you're no longer bridging from a solution deck. The repo is real, most of what it needed has already been read once, end to end, and the gaps that remain (§16.2's corrections, §16.4's contradictions) are *knowable* — which, per §7, means they're closeable. This document is only useful if you actually close them, not just read that they exist.

The quality ceiling is set by you. So set it high, and hold it when it's inconvenient.

content.content:
# Zimmermann - Salesforce PWA Kit (Production)

> **STRICT RULE — TypeScript only inside `overrides/`.**
> Every file created or modified under `overrides/` **must** use `.ts` or `.tsx`.
> `.js` and `.jsx` files are not acceptable here, including theme files, stories, and config modules.
> Run `npx tsc --noEmit` before finishing any task that touches `overrides/`.

Production storefront for www.zimmermann.com, a luxury Australian fashion brand. Must be robust and secure and SEO-friendly. See [.docs/architecture.md](.docs/architecture.md) for stack overview, overrides pattern, component organisation, and key paths.

Tier classifications and protected-file lists live in [.claude/rules/](.claude/rules/) — loaded automatically per session. Custom slash commands for scaffolding and review live in [.claude/skills/](.claude/skills/).

## Branch Rules

**At session start, always run `git branch --show-current`.** If the output is `develop` or `main`, stop immediately — do not make any changes.

| Branch | Branched from | Merges to | Allowed? | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `feature/*` | `develop` | `develop` | ✅ Yes | Primary working context for new work |
| `fix/*` | `develop` | `develop` | ✅ Yes | Non-urgent bug fixes. Mechanically identical to `feature/*` — naming is for commit hygiene |
| `release/*` | `develop` | `main` **and** `develop` | ⚠️ Supervised | Plan-first + confirm-every-edit required. Code logic fixes must use a `fix/release-*` sub-branch |
| `fix/release-{version}-*` | the `release/*` branch | the `release/*` branch, then forward-merged to `develop` once the release ships | ✅ Yes | Only path for code logic fixes on a release. PR targets the release branch; SIT gate runs against the PR. Treated like `feature/*` on the sub-branch itself — the "Supervised" plan-first + confirm-every-edit rules apply only to direct edits on the `release/*` branch |
| `hotfix/*` | `main` | `main` **and** `develop` | ✅ Yes | Urgent production fixes only. Tier 1 rules still apply. Must be back-merged to `develop` to prevent drift |
| `develop` | — | — | ❌ Never | Human commits only |
| `main` | — | — | ❌ Never | Human commits only |

> **On `release/*` or `hotfix/*` branches you MUST read [.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md](.docs/releaseBranchesRules.md) before any action.** It holds the supervised-edit rules (plan-first, confirm-every-edit, `fix/release-*` sub-branch flow) and the GitFlow back-merge rules that apply in addition to the Hard Rules below. On `feature/*` and `fix/*`, ignore it.

## Hard Rules

1. **Never operate on `develop` or `main`** branches.
2. **Never modify a Tier 1 file** without the developer explicitly naming it in the prompt and confirming owner approval — unless the verified-session exception in [Tier 1 Approval](#tier-1-approval--how-its-actually-enforced) applies. See [.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md](.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md).
3. **Never modify `overrides/app/theme/foundation/`** — all design token changes go through the UI designer.
4. **Never modify `overrides/app/ssr.js`, `config/default.js`, `config/sites.js`, `worker/main.js`, or `.github/workflows/`.**
5. **Never refactor upward.** Fixing a bug in a component does not mean touching the hook or utility it calls.
6. **Never rename or move a shared hook or component.**
7. **Never add or remove packages** from `package.json` without integration team approval. When approved, always use `npm install` rather than editing `package.json` directly.
8. **Never modify test configuration files** (`vitest.config.*`, `playwright.config.*`, `.storybook/`, `tests/lighthouserc.js`).
9. **Never delete files** without being explicitly asked in the current prompt. You may propose deletion and let a human confirm.
10. **Never touch more than one protection tier** in a single change without stopping to confirm scope with the developer.
11. **Never assume a hook is safe to modify** because it has a simple name — check the frozenFiles list first.
12. **When requirements are unclear, ask one clarifying question at a time.** Do not proceed with assumptions and do not batch questions. Wait for the answer before asking the next question or writing any code.
13. **Never use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`** on `release/**`, `main`, or `develop`. This flag bypasses all edit confirmations and is only permitted in CI automation contexts, never in interactive developer sessions on shared or protected branches.
14. **Never reference code from a later sprint.** Check [.docs/memory/sprintScope.md](.docs/memory/sprintScope.md) before scoping any new work. If a task depends on a component, hook, or integration that belongs to a later sprint, stop and ask whether to build a placeholder or whether that sprint is already complete.
15. **Never create a git commit, push to remote, or open/close a PR** without the developer explicitly requesting it in the current prompt. Resuming from a session summary, a task list, or a "natural next step" is not an instruction to commit — wait for an explicit ask.

## Tier 1 Approval — How It's Actually Enforced

Claude Code's confirmation prompt before touching a Tier 1 file (Hard Rule #2) is a workflow
safeguard, not the security boundary — it can't be, since it only governs what Claude itself
does, not what any other tool or a direct `git push` can do. The real enforcement is server-side:

- [CODEOWNERS](../CODEOWNERS) routes every Tier 1 path to `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`, a
  real GitHub org team.
- Branch protection on `develop`/`main`/`release/**` requires an approving code-owner review
  before merge — this is the actual gate, enforced natively by GitHub with no Actions
  involvement, so it can't be affected by a broken or delayed CI run.
- `.github/workflows/protected-file-guard.yml`'s `tier1-guard` job posts a loud warning and an
  owner-contact-map on any PR touching a Tier 1 path. It is **not** a required status check —
  GitHub locked down cross-run check-run updates in Feb 2025, which made a "hard-fail until
  approved, then flip to pass on review" required check impossible to implement reliably (a
  fresh commit is needed to re-evaluate it, since a later review can't flip an earlier run's
  result). The CODEOWNERS-based review requirement above is the real, working block.

Because the actual gate lives in GitHub, not in Claude's judgement, this file does not encode
personal names or email addresses as a bypass condition — a string in a shared, version-controlled
file is not an identity check; anyone (or any other Claude session) could satisfy it by typing it.
Instead, Claude may verify the real, authenticated identity behind the current session:

- Before pausing to ask for Tier 1 confirmation, run `gh api user --jq .login`, then check
  `gh api orgs/ZimmermannAU/teams/tier-1-approvers/members --jq '.[].login'` (or check for `admin`
  via `gh api repos/ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa/collaborators/<login>/permission`). If that GitHub
  login is a member of `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` or holds repo admin, Claude may proceed
  with the edit after stating which Tier 1 file is being touched and why — no separate
  confirmation message is required, since GitHub already recognises that account as an approver.
- If the authenticated login is **not** a member/admin, Claude must still stop per Hard Rule #2:
  name the file, and require the developer to secure an approving review from
  `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers` before the PR can merge. CODEOWNERS auto-requests that review
  and branch protection blocks the merge without it, regardless of what `tier1-guard` reports.
- This check only ever reduces *how many times Claude pauses to ask*. It changes nothing about
  what GitHub will actually allow to merge — that's deliberate, so a compromised or careless
  Claude session can't grant itself write access to a frozen file.

## Coding Task Workflow

Every coding task follows these four steps in order. Do not skip ahead — pause at the marked points and wait for the user.

1. **Clarify requirements.** Identify every gap, ambiguity, or contradiction in the request and the relevant `.docs/`. Confirm each one with the user before moving on — no assumptions. See Hard Rule #12: ask one question at a time.
2. **Plan.** State the files you intend to touch, *why* each one is being touched, and any base template files that will need to be copied to `overrides/`. Then **pause** and wait for the user to confirm the plan. See the **Minimal changes** rule below.
3. **Copy first (if any).** For every base template file identified in step 2, follow the **Copy-first rule** in the Rules section. Then **pause** and let the user test and stage the override files before any functional changes.
4. **Implement.** Make the planned modifications. Remove the `console.log` markers from step 3 once the user confirms the overrides are rendering.

## When to Stop and Ask a Human

| Trigger | Action |
|---|---|
| Task requires a Tier 1 file | Check the authenticated `gh` identity against `@ZimmermannAU/tier-1-approvers`/admin (see [Tier 1 Approval](#tier-1-approval--how-its-actually-enforced)). If verified, name the file and proceed. Otherwise stop and require named owner approval. |
| A shared hook needs its function signature changed | Stop. Requires a team RFC. |
| A new package dependency is needed | Stop. Integration team must approve. |
| Current branch is `develop` or `main` | Stop immediately. No changes. |
| Change affects more than one regional site config | Stop. Integration team sign-off required. |
| Change spans multiple protection tiers | Stop. Confirm scope with the developer before continuing. |
| Requirement is missing, ambiguous, contradictory, or unconfirmed in `.docs/` | Stop. Flag, propose, wait for approval (see Requirements section). |

## Multi-site & Routing
The SFCC sites are hard routing and config boundaries — **never bleed config across sites.** Never assume a storefront's routing, URL prefix, checkout ownership, or consent defaults without checking [.docs/prd/regional.md](.docs/prd/regional.md).

## Commands
- `npm start` — local dev at http://localhost:3000. **Do not run!** Ask the user to restart if needed.
- `npm run build`, `npx tsc --noEmit`, `npm run lint`, `npm run push` (Managed Runtime deploy)

## Accessibility
Target WCAG 2.2 AA. Fall back to 2.1 AA only where 2.2 is technically infeasible — document why.

## Rules

*Day-to-day code-writing conventions (file naming, component/hook/utility structure, imports, Storybook categorisation, types, no `any` policy) live in [.claude/rules/conventions.md](.claude/rules/conventions.md) and load automatically. The rules below are project-specific behaviours and security guardrails that don't fit there.*

- **No mocking:** All data must come from the live Commerce Cloud API via `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` hooks. No MSW or hardcoded fixtures in production paths.
- **Environment variables:** Never hardcode secrets, tokens, API keys, or credentials anywhere in the codebase. All such values must be defined in `.env` (local dev, gitignored) and set as platform environment variables on Managed Runtime for staging/prod. When adding a new env var: (1) add it to `.env` with the real value, (2) add it to `.env.sample` (with the value only if it is a non-secret public identifier, otherwise leave the value blank). Never put tokens, bearer credentials, DSNs, or licence keys in `.env.sample`.
- **Comments:** Do not remove existing commented-out code or comments (except when removing the corresponding code) — leave for the user to delete manually. (For *new* comments introduced in a PR, see conventions.md.)
- **Icons:** Use `overrides/app/components/icons` — this is the single source of truth for all icons (Zimmermann custom and base PWA). Do not import from `@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/icons` directly. If a required icon is missing from the overrides set, ask the user — do not substitute a visually different one.
- **Styling:** Chakra UI component props first; use a `.scss` file alongside the component only when Chakra props are insufficient. The `overrides/app/theme/` folder is the source of truth — brand tokens in `foundation/` (Tier 1), one file per component override in `components/` (Tier 2), composed in `index.ts`. Register a new component override in `theme/components/index.ts`.
- **Minimal changes:** Make the smallest change that fully achieves the task. Do not remove or replace existing base template functionality unless explicitly instructed. When a larger change (e.g., a refactor for cleanliness) seems beneficial, propose it and wait for user confirmation — never do it silently.
- **Copy-first rule:** For any task that requires overriding base template files that do not yet exist in `overrides/`, the very first step is to prepare all of them at once: (1) copy each file from `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/` to the mirrored path in `overrides/`, (2) convert each to TypeScript (`.ts`/`.tsx`) and update relevant imports, (3) run `npx tsc --noEmit`, (4) add a temporary `console.log` to each copied file identifying it (e.g. `console.log('[overrides] product-tile.tsx')`) so the user can verify the override is rendering instead of the base component, then **stop and present the converted files to the user to test**. Wait for the user to confirm the overrides are rendering before making any functional changes; remove the `console.log` statements once confirmed. Never skip this step or bundle it silently with functional changes.

## Consent & Marketing
- **Didomi:** Do not load any third-party script until Didomi consent is granted. Gate all analytics, marketing, and tracking scripts behind Didomi callbacks.
- **Marketing opt-in:** Unchecked by default on all storefronts except US (pre-checked). Sync opt-in state: FE → SFCC → Omneo → Emarsys.

*Per-storefront Didomi defaults, GTM/Enhanced Conversions setup, and Inside Chat rules: see [.docs/prd/regional.md](.docs/prd/regional.md).*

## Type Definitions
- **Component-specific prop types:** co-locate at the top of the component file.
- **Shared types** (Commerce Cloud entities, API responses, shared hook signatures): `overrides/app/types/` — split into `commerce.ts`, `components.ts`, `hooks.ts`, re-exported via `index.ts`.
- Don't re-declare types already exported by `commerce-sdk-isomorphic` or `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` — import them directly.

## Testing
Three layers: **Vitest** (unit logic) · **Storybook** `play` (component interactions) · **Playwright** (E2E). Write tests only where failure would be non-obvious or costly to debug — data mapping, integration boundaries, complex state, and pure logic that would survive a refactor invisibly if broken. Every UI component needs a `.stories.tsx`; every logic-heavy feature needs a `.test.ts` or a story `play`.

Full layer guidance, file layout, selector priority, and mocking policy: [.claude/rules/testing.md](.claude/rules/testing.md). (The no-MSW rule in Rules applies to production paths only.)

## Graceful Degradation
Each external system must fail independently — one outage must not break the whole page. Two defaults override any per-system behaviour: **fail closed on consent** (if consent state is unknown, load no third-party scripts), and **never silently substitute a different checkout, payment, or commerce flow** when an integration is down — surface an explicit error instead.

## Performance
Mobile page speed is a top priority. Every change that touches rendering, data fetching, or assets must not regress it.
- **LCP budget is tight (≤ 2s at p75 mobile)** — Defer every third-party script that isn't required for first paint. Anything loaded via Didomi callback (GTM, Optimizely, Inside Chat, Narvar EDD, reCAPTCHA, etc.) must not block LCP — use `defer`, `async`, or post-hydration injection. If a new third-party integration looks like it might land on the critical path, flag it before merging.
- **Images:** Always use lazy loading and serve correctly sized images. Never render full-resolution images at thumbnail size.
- **Code splitting:** Prefer dynamic `import()` for heavy components not needed on initial render.
- **Data fetching:** Avoid over-fetching — request only the fields you need. Waterfall requests are not acceptable; parallelise where possible.
- **Bundle size:** Do not introduce large dependencies without confirming with the user.
- **Dependencies:** Before implementing any feature that may require a third-party library, check `package.json` for what is already installed. Evaluate whether an existing dependency can satisfy the requirement. If a better third-party option exists, present the recommendation (existing vs. new, with trade-offs) and wait for user approval before installing anything.

## Gotchas
- **Theme runtime errors:** Custom components (e.g. `ListMenu`) must be defined in the theme object or destructuring will throw.
- **Commerce SDK types not importable:** Check `node_modules/commerce-sdk-isomorphic/dist/` for generated definitions, or declare a narrow local `type`.
- **Magento password migration:** Passwords were not migrated from Magento — all existing customers must reset at go-live. Do not assume any saved credentials exist. Account creation and login flows must handle this gracefully (CFD-013).

## Requirements
Requirements for this project are in `.docs/`, they must be strictly followed.
Before any code changes, verify logic against relevant `.docs/` files.

If a requirement is missing, ambiguous, or not yet confirmed — **stop, flag the ambiguity, propose a solution, and wait for user approval before proceeding.** Do not fill gaps with assumptions.

Verification: Start every task by briefly stating which doc/section you are following (e.g. "Implementing per auth.md section 2.1").

**Doc integrity:** Confirmed PRDs (`.docs/prd/`) and finalised Figma designs are the source of truth. If a user instruction contradicts either, pause immediately — cite the specific doc, section, and requirement ID — and ask the user whether the doc should be updated or the instruction is a deliberate override. Do not proceed silently either way. The same applies if you spot any improvement or conflict within the docs themselves.

## Living Memory
`.docs/memory/` is the project's persistent memory. Read [.docs/memory/projectState.md](.docs/memory/projectState.md) at the start of every session (or run `/session-start`). For what belongs in each memory file and when to update it, see the [session-start skill](.claude/skills/session-start/SKILL.md).

**Open items that block implementation** are listed under "Unresolved Dependencies" in [.docs/memory/projectState.md](.docs/memory/projectState.md). Ask the user before hard-coding assumptions about any of them.

# Code Conventions

Single source of truth for code-writing rules. Both [.claude/skills/new-component/](../skills/new-component/SKILL.md)
(when scaffolding) and [.claude/skills/code-quality/](../skills/code-quality/SKILL.md) (when auditing) reference this file.
Update here once — both skills, and (via [scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs](../../scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs) when ported)
all other AI tool configs, pick it up.

> Higher-level project rules live in [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md). Tier classifications live in
> [frozenFiles.md](./frozenFiles.md) and [protectedFiles.md](./protectedFiles.md).
> This file covers the *day-to-day code-writing* rules that apply to every file in a PR.

---

## General — every file in a PR

These apply to all `.ts`/`.tsx` files Claude creates or modifies, regardless of folder.

- **TypeScript only inside `overrides/`.** `.js`/`.jsx` is not acceptable here — see AGENTS.md.
- **No commented-out code blocks introduced by this PR** unless accompanied by an explicit
  strong reason in a comment immediately above. Existing comments are preserved per AGENTS.md —
  the rule is about *introducing* new dead code, not removing old.
- **No `console.log` or `console.error` calls** outside of error boundaries or explicit
  developer-tooling files. Use the project's logger when one is introduced.
- **No hardcoded design values.** Chakra UI props must use the Chakra token system — no
  hardcoded hex colours, no pixel values for spacing, no raw font sizes. Tokens belong in
  [overrides/app/theme/foundation/](../../overrides/app/theme/) (Tier 1).
- **React rules of hooks apply everywhere hooks are called.** Only call hooks at the top
  level of a component or another hook. No conditional, looped, or nested hook calls.
- **No `any`** without an inline comment explaining why a narrower type is impossible.
- **Prefer `type` over `interface`** for component props, shared shapes, and utility type aliases. Use `interface` only when declaration merging is genuinely needed.
- **Australian spelling** in Zimmermann-authored identifiers and copy (`colour`, `centre`,
  `organisation`). Override files keep upstream Salesforce spelling verbatim.
- **Apply DRY, KISS, and SOLID.** Don't repeat logic — extract to a shared utility or hook
  once the same pattern appears in two places. Prefer the simplest design that works; resist
  speculative abstractions. Keep modules to a single responsibility; split a file when it
  starts mixing concerns.
- **No magic numbers or strings.** Any literal value with semantic meaning — pixel
  thresholds, retry counts, country codes, feature flag names, status strings, error
  codes — must be a named constant (`const MAX_RETRIES = 3`) or live in a config/enum
  module. Excepted: `0`, `1`, `-1` in obvious idiomatic uses, and string literals that *are*
  the value (e.g. CSS class names, JSX text).
- **Payment credentials — never logged, never persisted client-side.** Gift card numbers,
  gift card PINs, credit card PANs, CVVs and similar secrets must not appear in any
  `console.*` call, Sentry breadcrumb / event, GTM dataLayer push, analytics event, MRT
  access log, or response body returned to the browser beyond a masked form. Never store
  them in `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB, or cookies — form state lives in
  React only and is cleared on unmount. Submit them in the POST **body**, never as a
  query string (URLs end up in MRT access logs, browser history, Referer headers). After
  submit, render only the serial portion (e.g. `••••••••1234`). Do not add body-logging
  middleware on routes that carry these fields. Logger and Sentry `beforeSend` must
  redact them. See [.docs/prd/giftcards.md §10](../../.docs/prd/giftcards.md) for the
  GiveX-specific rationale (only the card's serial portion may be displayed or logged).

---

## File naming and folder structure

- **Zimmermann-authored files and folders:** `camelCase` (e.g. `productTile.tsx`,
  `useWishlist.ts`, `formatPrice.ts`).
- **Override files (mirroring a base Salesforce file):** keep the original kebab-case
  filename and folder name exactly (e.g. `product-tile.tsx`). This makes the origin of a
  file obvious at a glance.
- **Component folder layout:** each component lives in its own folder under
  [overrides/app/components/](../../overrides/app/components/). Use `index.tsx` for the
  component itself so imports stay clean:

  ```
  overrides/app/components/productTile/
    index.tsx              ← the component
    index.stories.tsx      ← Storybook story
    index.test.ts          ← Vitest (only if logic-heavy)
    types.ts               ← only if props/types are shared with sibling files
    productTile.scss       ← only if Chakra props are insufficient
  ```

  Import as `import ProductTile from '.../components/productTile'`.

---

## Components

- **Named export** matches the folder name (e.g. `productTile/` exports `ProductTile`).
  No default exports of anonymous functions.
- **Props type name** matches the component name: `ProductTileProps` for `ProductTile`,
  `TopNavProps` for `TopNav`.
- **Props type placement:**
  - *Default:* declare the `Props` type at the top of the component file.
  - *Move to `types.ts` in the same folder* only when (a) the type is consumed by sibling
    files (story, test, sub-components) **or** (b) it exceeds ~30 lines and mixes with
    other shared types worth co-locating.
  - The trigger is *shared consumption*, not line count alone.
- **JSDoc** is required on:
  - Any component used by ≥2 callers (shared components — typically Tier 2 in
    [protectedFiles.md](./protectedFiles.md)).
  - Any exported hook.
  - Any utility function with non-obvious behaviour.

  Leaf components used by a single page don't need JSDoc — the prop type is sufficient.
- **Callback props** follow `onEventName` (e.g. `onAddToCart`, `onClose`).
- **Required props are non-optional;** optional props use `?` — no `| undefined` unions
  for "I forgot to mark it optional."
- **No commerce state hooks inside leaf components.** `useCurrentBasket`,
  `useCurrentCustomer`, etc. belong in pages or container components — accept data as props.

---

## Hooks

- **File extension** is `.ts` (no JSX in a hook file).
- **Exported function name** matches the filename: `useWishlist.ts` exports `useWishlist`.
- **Parameters and return value are typed** — no implicit `any`, no missing return type.
- **JSDoc** is required on every exported hook, including a `@returns` description.

---

## Utilities

- **Pure functions** — no side effects unless clearly intentional and called out in a comment.
- **No imports from `overrides/app/hooks/`** — utilities must not depend on hooks
  (it's the other direction).
- **Vitest required** when the utility has ≥1 conditional branch or performs ≥1
  transformation (currency, locale, mapping, parsing, etc.). Trivial re-exports or
  one-liners don't need a test.

---

## Storybook

Storybook is the canonical place to view components in isolation. Keep it browsable —
a flat 200-story sidebar is unusable.

### When a story is required

- **Required** for any component exported from its folder under `overrides/app/components/`
  or `overrides/app/pages/` (i.e. anything another file imports).
- **Not required** for purely internal sub-components that only render inside one parent
  (e.g. `productTile/priceRow.tsx` used only by `productTile/index.tsx`). Cover their
  variants via the parent's stories.
- Pages get a story showing the full assembly with representative props — not a story per
  sub-section.

### Categorisation

Story `title` drives the sidebar tree. Pick the first matching category:

| Category | What goes here |
|---|---|
| `Foundation/` | Design tokens — Colour, Typography, Spacing, Icons, Shadows |
| `Elements/` | Generic building blocks — both display (Badge, Tag, Link, Avatar, Skeleton) and interactive controls (Button, Input, Checkbox, Select). Tiebreaker: *can it be used outside a form?* → `Elements/`. |
| `Layout/` | Global chrome, navigation, and structural components — Header, Footer, DrawerMenu, ListMenu, Breadcrumb, Pagination, Seo |
| `Commerce/` | Commerce-specific shared components — ProductTile, OrderSummary, PromoCode, DisplayPrice, SwatchGroup |
| `Forms/` | Composed form assemblies — AddressForm, CheckoutContactForm, NewsletterSignup |
| `Pages/` | Full page assemblies — PDP, PLP, Cart, Checkout, Account |
| `Contentful/` | CMS-driven components — HeroBanner, RichText, ContentBlock. Use mock Contentful data in stories so variants are visible without a live CMS connection. |

Naming convention: singular for a concept or proper noun (`Foundation`, `Commerce`, `Layout`, `Contentful`); plural for a collection (`Elements`, `Forms`, `Pages`).

Examples:

```ts
export default { title: 'Commerce/ProductTile' }      // ✅
export default { title: 'Layout/Header' }             // ✅
export default { title: 'Elements/Button' }           // ✅
export default { title: 'Pages/PDP' }                 // ✅
export default { title: 'Elements/DisplayPrice' }     // ❌ — eCommerce specific, use Commerce/
export default { title: 'Primitives/Button' }         // ❌ — use Elements/
```

When in doubt: ask "what does this component *know* about?" Commerce → `Commerce/`,
CMS-driven → `Contentful/`, nothing domain-specific → `Elements/`, page-level composition → `Pages/`.

### Story content

- Every story file has a `Default` named export.
- Add named exports for meaningful states (`Loading`, `OutOfStock`, `WithDiscount`) — not
  for every possible prop combination.
- `play` functions only when there's interactive behaviour worth asserting; otherwise the
  story is purely visual.

---

## Imports

- **No circular imports** — if file A imports from file B, B must not import from A
  (check one level deep).
- **No `../../../..` chains longer than 3 levels** — flag for path-alias review.
- **No imports from internal `node_modules/@salesforce/...` source paths** — use the
  package's published entrypoints (`@salesforce/retail-react-app/...`).
- **No imports from a later-sprint feature** — cross-check
  `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md`.

# Testing Conventions

Three layers, three purposes. **Do not duplicate coverage across layers** — pick the cheapest layer that proves the behaviour.

| Layer | Tool | What it covers | File pattern | CI gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | Vitest | Pure logic, data mapping, transforms, hook behaviour in isolation | `*.test.ts` co-located with the source | Every PR (`qa.yml`) |
| Component interaction | Storybook `play` | User-facing interactions in a single component (clicks, form fills, focus management) | `*.stories.tsx` `play` function | Every PR (`qa.yml`) |
| E2E | Playwright | Full user journeys across pages, multi-region, integration boundaries | `e2e/tests/**/*.spec.{ts,js}` | Every PR (`qa.yml`) — desktop + mobile Chromium against localhost/dev API; BrowserStack multi-browser on `release/**` only |

> Higher-level project rules: [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md) > Testing. Day-to-day file conventions: [conventions.md](./conventions.md). This file describes **how** to write tests at each layer.

---

## What to test (and what to skip)

Write tests where failure would be **non-obvious** or **costly to debug**:

- ✅ Data mapping: Contentful → component props, locale/currency transforms, SFCC payload → view model
- ✅ Integration boundaries: Global-e pricing/tax logic, checkout ownership branching, consent gating
- ✅ Complex state: cart mutations, consent state changes, multi-step flows, optimistic-update rollback
- ✅ Pure logic that would survive a refactor invisibly if broken
- ❌ Re-exports, one-line passthroughs, type-only helpers
- ❌ Storybook visual snapshots — Chromatic/Loki belongs in a separate budget, not Vitest
- ❌ The framework — don't test that React renders, that Chakra applies styles, or that React Query caches

---

## Layer 1 — Vitest (unit)

### File layout

Co-located with the source, `.test.ts` suffix, never `.spec.ts`:

```
overrides/app/utils/formatPrice.ts
overrides/app/utils/formatPrice.test.ts
overrides/app/hooks/useCurrency.ts
overrides/app/hooks/useCurrency.test.ts
```

Components use `index.test.ts` next to `index.tsx` in the component folder
(see [conventions.md](./conventions.md) > Components).

### Structure

- `describe` blocks group related cases; `test` (or `it`) for individual cases.
- **Arrange → Act → Assert** pattern, one behaviour per test.
- Test names describe the behaviour, not the implementation: `"converts AUD to USD using the latest Global-e rate"` not `"calls convertCurrency"`.
- Use `beforeEach` for setup; clear mocks with `vi.clearAllMocks()` after each test.

### Mocking

- **Inline mock objects** for isolated unit tests — define plain JS objects right in the test file.
- **`vi.mock()`** for module-level stubs. Mock the smallest possible surface: a single function, not a whole module, when feasible.
- **MSW** is allowed for cross-functional integration tests (multiple modules wired together). Production paths must never depend on MSW — see AGENTS.md > Rules > "No mocking."
- Do not mock the thing under test; do not assert on internal implementation calls when an output assertion would do.

### Commerce SDK hooks

Hooks that call `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` (e.g. `useCurrentBasket`, `useCurrentCustomer`) need a `QueryClientProvider` and `CommerceApiProvider` wrapper. Build a small `renderWithProviders` helper in `overrides/app/test-utils/` rather than duplicating wrapper boilerplate per test.

### What NOT to write at this layer

- Visual rendering — that's Storybook
- Cross-page navigation — that's Playwright
- Real network calls — never; use MSW or stubbed hooks

---

## Layer 2 — Storybook `play` (component interaction)

### When to use `play`

Every UI component has a `*.stories.tsx` (see [conventions.md](./conventions.md) > Storybook). Add a `play` function when there is **interactive behaviour worth asserting**:

- Form validation triggers on blur / submit
- Disclosure (accordion, drawer, modal) opens / closes via keyboard + mouse
- Focus moves correctly through a flow
- A controlled input's onChange wires through to the rendered output

If the story is purely visual (renders different prop combinations), no `play` is needed.

### Pattern

```tsx
import {expect, userEvent, within} from '@storybook/test'

export const SubmitDisabledUntilValid: Story = {
    play: async ({canvasElement}) => {
        const canvas = within(canvasElement)
        const submit = canvas.getByRole('button', {name: /submit/i})
        await expect(submit).toBeDisabled()
        await userEvent.type(canvas.getByLabelText(/email/i), 'name@example.com')
        await expect(submit).toBeEnabled()
    }
}
```

- Always query through `within(canvasElement)` — never reach into `document` directly.
- Use **`getByRole`** with an accessible name as the first-choice selector. Fall back to `getByLabelText` for form fields, `getByText` last.
- Don't import `userEvent` from `@testing-library/user-event` — use the Storybook re-export so the action is logged in the timeline.

### What NOT to write at this layer

- Multi-page flows — that's Playwright
- Heavy API mocking — keep stories visual, push integration assertions to Playwright

---

## Layer 3 — Playwright (E2E)

### Workflow

E2E tests follow the **three-stage gherkin-first workflow** (see [.claude/skills/qa-generate/](../skills/qa-generate/SKILL.md)):

1. Claude (or any developer) drafts a `.feature` file with Gherkin scenarios
2. Lead QA validates in plain English — **no Playwright code is written until sign-off**
3. Playwright spec is generated only after the `.feature` is approved

This prevents "technically correct tests of the wrong behaviour."

### File layout

```
e2e/features/         # Gherkin .feature files — source of truth, reviewed by Lead QA
e2e/fixtures/         # multi-region fixtures keyed by SITE_ID
e2e/support/
  helpers/            # shared helpers (auth, basket setup)
  pages/              # Page Object Model classes (BasePage, CheckoutPage, …)
e2e/tests/zimm/       # generated Playwright specs, mirroring features/
```

Spec filename convention: `SFCC-NNN_short-description.<priority>.spec.ts`
(`.p0.` runs in the Digital SIT gate on `release/**`; all specs run on every feature PR against localhost).

### Multi-region fixtures

Build SITE_ID-keyed fixtures from day one — Zimmermann has 7 storefronts across 6 regions (AU, US — combining domestic and international, UK, EU domestic, EU international, HK, ME) and 11 active locales. Do not retrofit. A test that hardcodes a region or currency cannot survive the rollout.

```ts
test.describe('Guest checkout', () => {
    for (const site of SITES) {
        test(`completes on ${site.id}`, async ({page}) => { ... })
    }
})
```

### Page Object Model

Selector priority — **enforce in code review**. Select elements the way real users (and assistive tech) perceive them:

1. **Accessible selectors** — role with accessible name, label, placeholder, visible text. `getByRole('button', {name: 'Add to bag'})`, `getByLabelText('Email')`, `getByPlaceholderText('Search')`, `getByText('Sale')`. First choice — these double as continuous a11y checks.
2. **Semantic selectors** — standard HTML attributes when no accessible selector applies. `getByAltText('Profile picture')`, `getByTitle('Close modal')`.
3. **Test IDs** — `data-testid` only when the element has no semantic meaning or text content (dynamic containers, canvas elements, loading spinners, complex layout blocks).

Never select by tag name, class name, or DOM position. The priority order keeps tests close to user experience and minimises `data-testid` clutter in the DOM, while still allowing a reliable fallback where semantics genuinely don't exist.

### What NOT to write at this layer

- Pure logic — that's Vitest
- Component interaction in isolation — that's Storybook `play`
- Network-mocked flows — Playwright always hits real SFCC APIs (dev org on feature PRs, SIT on the release gate). Do not stub network calls in Playwright tests.

`vitest.config.*`, `playwright.config.*`, `.storybook/`, `lighthouserc.js` are
**frozen** ([frozenFiles.md](./frozenFiles.md)). Do not modify them in a feature PR — config drift breaks every contributor's harness. Changes go through the Integration team.

scripts/contentful/content-types/
