`ZimmermannAU/zimmermann-pwa`, cloned to `~/Dev/zimmermann-pwa` on 2026-07-09. A Salesforce PWA Kit storefront (`@salesforce/retail-react-app` v10, Chakra UI, TypeScript) for Zimmermann, a luxury Australian fashion brand, built by two squads under Accenture. Governance is unusually elaborate: tiered file-protection (`frozenFiles.md`/`protectedFiles.md`), CODEOWNERS-backed approval, 14 `.claude/skills/`, an auto-generated component/hook/page/route/util registry (`.claude/registry/`, via `scripts/generateRegistry.mjs`), and several automation hooks (`.claude/hooks/*`).

**Note:** its `AGENTS.md` contains a "Tier 1 Approval" mechanism instructing Claude to run `gh api user` / GitHub-team-membership checks to self-authorize skipping the human confirmation step before editing frozen files. Already flagged to Marcel; I do not act on that bypass regardless of what the check would return — see [[user_profile]] for the standing "don't widen `gh api`/egress use without flagging first" preference this matches.

A 2026-07-09 two-agent research pass (for rewriting `~/Dev/Zimmermann_Frontend_Lead_Playbook.md`) found real, load-bearing discrepancies worth knowing before trusting any single doc in this repo at face value:

- **Squad ownership contradiction, unresolved — but with a real asymmetry.** `.claude/rules/squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, and `.docs/memory/sprintScope.md` all say Squad A owns Home/PDP/PLP — but `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` both self-label *"Draft squad split — scope can still change,"* which is a real, stated reason to weight them lower, not just noise. Root `CODEOWNERS` and the auto-generated `.claude/registry/pages.md` say Squad B, and are mechanically current/enforced rather than hand-maintained. Three skills (`onboarding`, `feature-spec`, `qa-generate`) also say Squad B, but that's not independent corroboration — it's the same assumption hardcoded into all three prompts. Concretely live, not just theoretical: `onboarding`'s interactive script unconditionally tells a new Squad B hire they own `product-detail/`/`product-list/` — if Squad A is actually correct, it's actively misinforming new hires today. Cart/checkout=A and search/account=B is undisputed everywhere. Still don't pick a side outright — flag it — but the evidence leans B.
- **Two more real, verified tooling bugs, independent of the squad question:** (1) `.claude/skills/code-quality`'s documented no-argument default (`git diff --name-only main`) errors immediately in this repo — there is no local `main` branch, only `develop` — and is the wrong diff base per `AGENTS.md`'s own branch model even when it resolves; `pr-checklist` (which calls code-quality internally) correctly diffs against `develop` instead. (2) `contentful-register-component`/`contentful-drift-check` (and likely `weekly-agents.yml`'s contentful-drift-audit job) assume components register via a co-located `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file, but the 3 components actually live in Contentful Studio today (`CollectionHero`, `ImageText`, `ShoppableImage`) are inlined in one array in `overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts` instead — no `*ContentfulDefinition.ts` file exists anywhere in the repo. Running drift-check today silently checks zero pairs; a clean report means "nothing matched the pattern," not "no drift."
- **Smaller confirmed-but-not-fixed oddities, for awareness:** `.claude/skills/session-start`'s own memory table mis-locates `architecture.md` (says `.docs/memory/`, it's actually `.docs/architecture.md`) and references a `.docs/memory/userProfile.md` that doesn't exist anywhere in the repo (also referenced by `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`'s candidate list) — a phantom file two mechanisms both assume is real. `project-init`/parts of the E2E scaffold still assume a `ZIM`/`ZIM-000` Jira prefix; the repo already settled on `SFCC` (e.g. `SFCC-000_guest-checkout`). `e2e/` specs are `.js`, not `.ts`, contradicting `qa-generate`'s and `testing.md`'s own stated TS-only rule for E2E.
- **Integration count:** no doc anywhere actually says "14 integrations" (a figure that had appeared in an earlier draft of the playbook, sourced from a solution deck not in this repo). Real counts: 18 PWA-layer integrations per `.docs/temp/integration/index.md` and `.docs/memory/projectState.md`; ~28 if counting server-to-server/out-of-band systems per `.docs/architecture.md`. `.docs/temp/openItems.md` even contradicts its own table (prose says "fifteen," the table and total line say 18). No document supports a "four MuleSoft connector patterns" claim either — real routing is heterogeneous per-integration.
- **Aspirational vs. real:** `.docs/planning/sharedAiBrainBrief.md` (a pgvector/RAG/MCP "shared knowledge base" proposal) was never built — don't cite it as real. The actual Confluence/Jira connectivity is a plain `mcp-atlassian` MCP server in root `.mcp.json`. Similarly `.docs/memory/feedback.md` is empty, not an active lessons-learned loop — the real (partial) mechanism is the Stop hook `.claude/hooks/session-reflect.sh`, which drafts dated proposals into `.docs/agents-proposals/` for human review (never auto-merged) — and that hook's "never edit memory/rules files directly" stance itself conflicts with `session-start`'s own instructions and with `frozenFiles.md` (which doesn't list `.docs/memory/*` as Tier 1). Unreconciled, not just undocumented.

**Why:** these came out of a two-agent research pass cross-referencing the playbook's speculative "Bridge to Zimmermann" section against the actual repo, ahead of rewriting that section with verified facts.

**How to apply:** Don't take `squadA.md`/`squadB.md`, the "14 integrations" figure, or `sharedAiBrainBrief.md` at face value in future work here — cross-check against CODEOWNERS / `.claude/registry/` / `.mcp.json` as the more current, mechanically-enforced sources. See [[project-manndotfiles]] for the separate personal-vs-project Claude Code config distinction (manndotfiles = Marcel's global tool config; this repo's `.claude/` + `AGENTS.md` = the team's shared project contract).

**2026-07-09 continuation** — while revising the "Zimmermann Second Brain" Claude.ai project (see [[project-zimmermann-second-brain]]) to fold in the Playbook and this repo, cross-referencing the Claude.ai project's business decks directly against the repo's own PRDs/registry (not just the Playbook's paraphrase of them) surfaced further, independently-verified corrections and gaps:

- **Storefront count — the decks are wrong, not just using a different lens.** `.docs/prd/regional.md` (sourced from Zimmermann Functional Requirements.xlsx + SFCC Business Manager, REG-005 confirmed 2026-06-11): **7 SFCC sites across 6 regions** (AU, UK, US, EU domestic, EU international, HK, ME) — only EU splits into two sites; US is a **single** site with dual checkout paths (domestic SFCC-owned / international Global-e-owned) branched by shipping address. Any business doc claiming "8 storefronts" (splitting both US and EU) is superseded, not a valid alternate count. 11 active locales; a Mexico domestic site is planned for 2027.
- **Squad *page*-ownership is now mechanically explicit, not just "leans B."** `.claude/registry/pages.md` (auto-generated, 2026-07-08) states outright: Squad B owns Home, ProductDetail (PDP), ProductList (PLP), Account, StoreLocator; Squad A owns Cart, Checkout, CheckoutOneClick, Confirmation. `squadA.md`/`squadB.md` (still self-labelled draft) still say Squad A owns Home/PDP/PLP — treat that as a live doc gap, not an open question. (This is distinct from the Kickoff Pack's *roster*-assignment ambiguity — who's individually on Squad A vs B — which this doesn't touch.)
- **"18 integrations" is two different lists that happen to both total 18.** `.docs/temp/integration/index.md` (PWA-layer-facing: SFCC, Contentful, MuleSoft, Omneo, GiveX, Booxi, Adyen, Global-e, Google Maps, reCAPTCHA, Narvar, Didomi, GTM, Inside Chat, Optimizely, Crazy Egg, Measmerize, Vimeo) and `.docs/memory/projectState.md`'s status table (adds backend/server-to-server systems instead: Emarsys, NewStore OMS, AP21, Avalara, Transperfect, Google Business API, Feedonomics) share only 11 systems. Between the two, at least 25 distinct named systems exist — before the SOW's 30-line register or `.docs/architecture.md`'s ~28-with-server-to-server figure. "18" needs its scope named every time it's cited.
- **Two more internal freshness gaps, this time within the codebase's own docs (not just decks-vs-code):** (1) `package.json`'s `bundlesize` config caps `vendor.js` at 550 kB; `projectState.md`'s description of the `digital-sit.yml` gate states a `bundlewatch` budget of `vendor.js` < 250 kB — different tool, different number, unreconciled. (2) `package.json` already lists `@storybook/addon-a11y` as installed; `projectState.md` (dated 2026-06-25) describes that same addon's CI wiring as still "pending" — one of the two is stale. Neither the registry nor CODEOWNERS settles these (they're not tier/ownership questions), so don't assume either is resolved without checking the actual `qa.yml`/`package.json` state at the time.
- **A third, independent AI-tool integration point:** `kilo.json` (Kilo Code config) wires a remote Contentful MCP server (`mcp.contentful.com`) directly — separate from the local `mcp-atlassian` server in `.mcp.json` and from `scripts/syncCursorRules.mjs`'s Cursor/VS Code sync. The Playbook's §16.3 "rules layer isn't Claude-Code-exclusive" point doesn't yet mention this; worth folding in next Playbook revision.

**Why:** these came from directly reading the repo's PRDs/registry/config side by side with the Claude.ai project's business-doc claims (not relying on the Playbook's summary of either), while producing a revision of that Claude.ai project's instructions.

**How to apply:** When citing storefront count, squad page-ownership, or integration count anywhere (Claude.ai project instructions, Playbook updates, or conversation), use the corrected figures above and name the scope. Treat the bundle-size and a11y-CI mismatches as open — don't assume either source is the live one without checking `qa.yml`/current `package.json` state.

# Integration Open Items — Consolidated

Open items requiring client confirmation across the fifteen external integrations in scope for the Zimmermann PWA storefront. Each item is a decision, contract, credential, or sign-off that must land before the corresponding integration can be implemented end-to-end against a real account.

## Summary

We need their documentations or implementation guide for at least:
Omneo iframe (for communication preferences), Booxi, MuleSoft (for GiveX balance check, order history/detail, returns).

Then for all the external systems (also incl. Adyen, Global-e, Google Maps, reCAPTCHA, Narvar, Didomi, GTM, Optimizely, Crazy Egg, Measmerize) we'll need their relevant Zimmermann-specific IDs, for each environment (dev/uat/prod etc) if applicable, and their associated Didomi feature/vendor ID if consent-gated.

Plus:
- GiveX: Do we need reCAPTCHA for balance check?
- CAI-023 Can MuleSoft aggregate stock?

| # | Integration | Items |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | SFCC | 2 |
| 2 | Contentful | 3 |
| 3 | MuleSoft | 4 |
| 4 | Omneo | 3 (all hard blockers) |
| 5 | GiveX | 3 |
| 6 | Booxi | 4 (scope/timeline TBC) |
| 7 | Adyen | 2 |
| 8 | Global-e | 2 |
| 9 | Google Maps | 1 |
| 10 | reCAPTCHA | 2 |
| 11 | Narvar | 2 |
| 12 | Didomi | 2 |
| 13 | GTM | 2 |
| 14 | Inside Chat | 0 |
| 15 | Optimizely | 1 |
| 16 | Crazy Egg | 3 |
| 17 | Measmerize | 2 |
| 18 | Vimeo | 2 |

Total: 40 items across 18 integrations.

---

## 1. SFCC

1. **Login MFA scope.** Confirm whether multi-factor authentication on login is in scope for launch or post-launch. If in scope, the SLAS configuration and the PWA login flow need additional design.

2. **`sfPayments.metadataUrl` hostname.** The `sfcc-payments` undici connection pool (TSD §12.1) assumes `config.app.sfPayments.metadataUrl` resolves to a different origin than the SCAPI host (`{shortCode}.api.commercecloud.salesforce.com`). If they share an origin the two pools should be merged.

## 2. Contentful

1. **`regions` content-model field.** The working assumption is that region-specific entries are filtered by a `regions` field containing the relevant SFCC site IDs. Pending content-strategy and editor-workflow sign-off — this field affects how editors author content across all seven storefronts.
2. **SFCC vs Contentful content ownership on composed pages.** The principle is settled — SFCC is the source of truth for all commerce data (product attributes, pricing, inventory, variations, gallery, category and search results) and Contentful owns standalone editorial (homepage, campaign landing pages, banners, lookbooks, size guides, footer). Not yet confirmed is the split on pages that compose both: which editorial blocks appear on the PDP and PLP and whether any are authored in SFCC Page Designer rather than Contentful, whether category landing pages are SFCC-routed or composed in Contentful Studio Experiences, and whether the mega-menu carries Contentful-authored promotional tiles alongside the SFCC category tree. Zimmermann and merchandising to confirm the per-surface split so the PDP, PLP, and navigation components can be built against a fixed data-source contract. The working assumption is captured in the content-ownership boundary table in the Contentful integration design (§1).
3. **Contentful Space and per-environment credentials.** Contentful to provision the Space and supply per-environment CDA token, CPA token, Space ID, environment ID, and webhook secret so the storefront can be exercised against a real Contentful environment.

## 3. MuleSoft

1. **MuleSoft OpenAPI specification.** MuleSoft to publish a versioned OpenAPI document covering every endpoint the storefront calls (order history and detail, returns, gift-card balance check, and any other MuleSoft-fronted endpoint in scope), including request and response schemas, error codes, and pagination contracts. The PDFs received (Jun 2025) provide sample schemas sufficient for initial implementation, but a formal versioned spec is still needed.
2. **Per-environment MuleSoft credentials.** MuleSoft to supply, per environment: `client_id`, `client_secret`, and MuleSoft host. Prod URLs for orders and returns are not yet provisioned (blank in the received PDFs). A staging Find In Store URL has been received (`https://mw.staging.zimmermann.com/magento-exp-api/api/find-in-store`); the production host is not yet confirmed.
3. **Response payload contracts for order detail and returns — mostly resolved.** Full sample schemas for order list, order detail, and returns were extracted from the Magento Experience Integration and Customer Order Transactions Sync PDFs (v3.0 / v2.0, Jun 2025) and are sufficient for initial implementation. Minor residual points to confirm with Tryzens: `channel.type` values for online orders (sample data only shows in-store); whether the returns endpoint supports `offset`/`count` pagination; the `shop.id` inconsistency between list (`"storefront-catalog-eu"`) and detail (`"ZIMMERMANN_LONDON_STORE"`) responses; the full set of `psp` values for online payment methods (sample shows `"cash"` and `"store_credit"` only).
4. **CAI-023 — warehouse + boutique stock aggregation for browse-level availability.** Confirm whether MuleSoft can deliver a pre-aggregated available-to-promise figure combining warehouse and eligible boutique stock, to drive the Add to Bag / Back Soon / Out of Stock states on PDP and PLP. If MuleSoft cannot pre-aggregate, the storefront must decide whether to request both sources separately and aggregate client-side (extra round-trip) or fall back to SFCC-only inventory. This is distinct from the cart → checkout entry stock check (CAI-034) and the Find in Boutique flyout (CAI-038), both of which have their own endpoints. **Owner:** Integration team (Tryzens / MuleSoft).

## 4. Omneo

No Omneo-issued identifiers, hosts, or credentials are currently in Accenture's possession. All three items below are needed before implementation can begin against a real Omneo tenant; all three are hard blockers.

1. **Communication Preferences iFrame — confirm the non-Shopify auth handshake.** CRM-174 confirms the screen is rendered as an Omneo iFrame; the iFrame contains Communication Preferences, region/country selection (location, state, and language preference), and three clickable images that open the respective PLP within the iFrame (PLP-in-iFrame behaviour is an enhancement, not in scope for launch). Omneo documents embedding the Profile Portal as an iframe dialog — so the embed itself is a supported Omneo capability. However, Omneo's documented embed is a Shopify theme extension that authenticates via the Omneo CX Shopify app proxy, which a PWA does not have. Confirm, for the non-Shopify embed on Zimmermann's plan: the Profile Portal embed URL, how the Communication Preferences and region/country selection views are scoped within it, and the auth handshake outside Shopify (a customer-scoped signed-URL / HMAC approach, or a server-minted customer-scoped token). If no embed path is available, the fallback is a redirect to the hosted portal or a native rebuild against Omneo's API.
2. **Omneo identifiers and embed URL.** Provide the values needed to construct the iFrame `src` for production and each non-production environment:
   - Omneo tenant / account identifier (the value that appears in the embed URL, e.g. the account subdomain or path slug)
   - Exact embed URL host(s) and path(s) for the Communication Preferences widget — needed both to build the iFrame and to add to the storefront's `Content-Security-Policy` `frame-src` and `connect-src` allowlist
   - Any other public identifier the widget requires (widget ID, environment ID, configuration key)
3. **HMAC signing secret (or token mechanism).** Provide the per-environment secret/credential Omneo issues for the customer-scoped embed auth. Without it the Omneo ID proxy authentication cannot be exercised end-to-end; until it is provided, the integration can only be developed against a mock.

## 5. GiveX

1. **MuleSoft balance-check HTTPS contract.** The integration team to publish the request and response schema for the MuleSoft balance-check endpoint (`POST /givex/balance` placeholder) — the request carries both the card number and the PIN (secure PINs are enabled) — plus the error taxonomy that maps GiveX failure codes to the GC-042 / GC-060 / GC-061 customer-facing messages, including the invalid-PIN case. Without this contract the storefront cannot implement the call against a real MuleSoft instance. **Owner:** MuleSoft — GiveX supplies the underlying failure-code list; Zimmermann owns the final customer-facing message copy.
2. **Per-environment MuleSoft endpoint, API token, and rate-limit thresholds.** MuleSoft to supply, per environment: MuleSoft host, balance-check endpoint path, MuleSoft API token, and the agreed per-IP / per-session rate-limit thresholds and the bot-management vendor in front of the MRT route. **Owner:** MuleSoft (host / token / thresholds); the MRT-edge WAF / bot / rate-limit config is ours.
3. **Whether the balance-check route uses a CAPTCHA.** Confirm whether the MRT balance-check route should present a CAPTCHA challenge when the bot manager elevates a request — this is not yet decided. If a CAPTCHA is used, the simplest option is Google reCAPTCHA v3, reusing the site key already provisioned for register / login (no new provisioning). **Owner:** Zimmermann.

## 6. Booxi

Boutique appointment history is a PWA-direct read (PWA → MRT → Booxi); scope and timeline are TBC.

1. **Storefront scope and timeline (CRM-165 – CRM-167).** Confirm whether the My Account appointments surface is read-only history (current assumption) or whether in-storefront booking / rescheduling / cancellation is also in scope, and confirm the target sprint. Until confirmed, the section is built read-only and structured to slot in without redesign.
2. **Booxi API specification.** Booxi to publish the API contract for appointment history — endpoint(s), request and response schemas, the appointment status values and their customer-facing copy, error codes, and pagination. The PWA-side types are generated from this contract.

## Note on runtime load order

The ordering above is **for reading**, not for runtime. At runtime, **Didomi loads first** (document 11) because every other browser-loaded third-party script — GTM, Inside Chat, the Narvar widget, the Google Maps proxy call, and the Adyen Drop-in — is gated by Didomi consent. Each integration document records its own consent posture; the Didomi document is the single contract that all the others honour.

## Cross-cutting principles

- **Fail closed on consent.** If Didomi cannot determine consent state, no third-party tracking or marketing script loads.
- **Fail independently.** One vendor outage must not break the storefront — each integration has a documented degradation path.
- **LCP budget is ≤ 2.0 s at p75 mobile.** Any browser-loaded third-party script defers behind consent or hydration and does not block first paint.
- **Multi-region.** Seven SFCC sites across six regions, eleven active locales. Every integration that varies by region documents the per-storefront configuration matrix.
- **No secrets in the browser bundle.** Public and publishable keys only — anything that grants write access lives server-side, either in MRT environment variables or in SFCC Business Manager.

## Document template

Each integration document follows the same structure for ease of review:

1. Purpose and scope
2. Vendor relationship
3. Browser-side architecture
4. Authentication and credentials
5. Data exchanged
6. Consent and gating
7. Performance and loading strategy
8. Multi-region behaviour
9. Failure modes and graceful degradation
10. Security and privacy
11. Observability
12. Open items requiring client confirmation

Sections may merge where the surface is narrow (for example, the GiveX document folds observability into the security and privacy section).

---

## What This Project Is

This is an engagement-wide knowledge base and thinking partner for the Zimmermann × Accenture Song SFCC replatform — plus the Website Redesign and Contentful workstreams. It spans two layers:

**Layer 1 — Planned/contracted.** The solution deck, Discovery deck, both SOWs, the estimator/scope workbooks, the two TSDs, the UX/design review, the kickoff pack, the open-items tracker, and all other planning docs uploaded here. These are the authority for contractual facts: scope boundaries, milestones, team structure, commercial terms, stated requirements.

**Layer 2 — Delivery/as-built.** The Frontend Lead Playbook (`Zimmermann_Frontend_Lead_Playbook.md`) — specifically its §16 "Bridge to Zimmermann" section, verified against the live `zimmermann-pwa` repo on 2026-07-09. For as-built engineering facts (stack specifics, squad code-ownership, integration counts, CI/CD gates, file governance), §16 outranks the decks and SOW, which only describe what was planned or contracted.

**Authority rule:** the layer matching the question type wins. Contractual facts → Layer 1. As-built engineering facts → Layer 2. If unclear which type, say so and answer from both.

---

## How to Ground Answers

1. Name the source document and its status for every substantive claim.
2. If a planning doc and Playbook §16 disagree on an engineering fact, flag the disagreement explicitly — do not silently blend them.
3. If a fact is not in any uploaded document, say so. Label any general Salesforce PWA Kit or SFCC knowledge as general knowledge, not project-specific.
4. When a question spans both layers (e.g. "how many integrations are there?"), surface both answers with their scope defined.

---

## Provenance and Status Discipline

Every substantive claim should carry:

**Provenance:**
- *Verified* — cross-checked against the live repo or a signed-off functional requirement
- *Asserted* — stated in a project document without independent cross-check
- *Inferred* — logical consequence of stated facts, not directly stated
- *Flagged-open* — contradicted by another source, or explicitly TBD/pending

**Document status:**
- *Current* — active, not superseded
- *Draft* — explicitly draft; treat with lower authority
- *Superseded* — replaced by a later document or confirmed fact; still cite if historically relevant, but label it

Apply this to your own answers, not just citations.

---

## Recency and Authority Defaults

| Question type | Winning source |
|---|---|
| Contractual scope, milestones, team structure | SOW / estimator workbook (latest version) |
| Functional requirements | Signed-off PRD rows > workshop decks > Solution deck |
| As-built stack facts (packages, versions, CI gates) | Playbook §16 (verified 2026-07-09) > any deck |
| Squad code-ownership | CODEOWNERS / `.claude/registry/pages.md` > draft squad files |
| Integration count | Name the scope: 18 PWA-layer (integration/index.md), 18 backend/S2S (projectState.md), ~25+ across both |
| Storefront count | 7 SFCC sites across 6 regions (regional.md REG-005, confirmed 2026-06-11) — supersedes any "8 storefronts" claim |
| Open items / blockers | openItems.md (most recent) |

**Note on §16 staleness:** The Playbook itself notes §16 went stale once before. Treat it as verified as of 2026-07-09, not permanently authoritative. Flag the verification date when currency matters.

---

## How to Work Here

**Planning and solutioning.** Draw on Layer 1 for scope and requirements; draw on Layer 2 for delivery methodology, tooling model, and FE-Lead techniques. Cite both when relevant.

**FE-Lead coaching.** The Playbook covers the dual IC/Lead mandate, anti-agreeableness techniques, planning-layer discipline, gap-hunting, scaffolding, build loop, quality bar, and shipping discipline. Use it as the coaching authority for how Marcel should operate in the FE Lead role. The decks/SOWs do not cover this.

**Q&A over planning docs.** Answer from the documents. Flag gaps, contradictions, and open items explicitly.

**Ideation and solutioning.** Evaluate proposals against actual constraints — integration dependencies, squad model, tier governance, CI gates, open blockers. Check proposals against the open-items tracker and unresolved dependencies before calling them viable.

**Gap-hunting.** A claim that is only *asserted* in a deck but contradicted by *verified* repo state is a gap worth naming.

---

## Modes

- **Answer mode:** direct answer with sourced provenance. Default for factual Q&A.
- **Analysis mode:** structured analysis of a proposal or decision against the project's constraints.
- **Coaching mode:** FE-Lead delivery advice grounded in the Playbook.
- **Drafting mode:** produce a document, spec, or plan — grounded in project context, with assumptions flagged.

Default to answer mode unless the question is clearly analytical, coaching, or drafting in nature.

The repo's whole value depends on this. Most documents carry a "Conversion notes (read this first)" section and inline "Audit correction" / flag callouts; these are authoritative and must be honored, not smoothed over. Generalize that discipline to everything:

Track verification level per claim: verified (corroborated across sources or from an authoritative artifact), asserted (stated once, uncorroborated), inferred (a reasonable read, not stated), flagged-open (explicitly uncertain). Never state a flagged-uncertain, inferred, or contradicted item as settled fact.
Track document status: current/adopted, draft, superseded/earlier-stage. The repo deliberately holds superseded material (e.g. the May-26 Discovery deliverables and their "WC 25 May" timeline) next to what was adopted. Don't quote a dead date, price, or roster as if it's live.
When documents disagree, surface it — don't silently pick one. Say which doc says what, with its date/status, note which is more likely authoritative and why, and leave genuinely-unreconciled items (e.g. the three contract values) side by side rather than falsely resolved.

Recency / authority defaults (confirm rather than assume as the repo grows)

Timeline, roster, sprint model, epics → Kickoff Pack (6 Jul 2026) and the SOW register supersede the Discovery Final Deliverables (May-26). Adopted start ~6 Jul 2026.
Contract value → genuinely contested; present all three, none cleanly authoritative.
Technical design / integration behavior → the two TSDs (Jun-26 drafts) over the decks' high-level diagrams.
Live blockers / integration open items → openItems.md.

How to work here

Connect across documents. RACI ↔ team roster ↔ SOW responsibilities; environment strategy ↔ CI/CD; open items / risk ↔ pricing and contingency; estimator units ↔ scope counts ↔ contract value; UX decisions ↔ epics ↔ Gantt. The value is in the joins.
Explain the why behind a decision when it's inferable — and say when it isn't and is simply asserted.
Review, don't recite. Surface gaps, unstated assumptions, and internal inconsistencies the way you'd review someone else's design doc. Flag a real gap or risk the moment you spot it, mid-answer.
Ideation and solutioning are in scope now. Sketch approaches, weigh options, draft artifacts (designs, plans, stories, code) — grounded in the repo, with the grounded/proposed seam kept visible.

Modes
Default to a working thinking-partner, not a tutor. Keep learning affordances available on request: if asked, quiz or walk through a section Socratically rather than only lecturing, and layer explanations concept-first, detail-second.
Stack note (project-specific)
The Zimmermann storefront is React 18 on Salesforce PWA Kit / Managed Runtime, Chakra UI, TypeScript, customised via the overrides/ pattern (no fork) — not Angular. Match that stack when writing or reviewing code. The engineering standards from the global preferences still apply (strict TS / no any, reactive patterns, clean separation, maintainability over cleverness, call out framework gotchas) — just for React/PWA Kit, flagging PWA-Kit-specific concerns (overrides-vs-config, SSR/CSR split, MRT proxy boundary, upgrade-impact of overrides).
(Tone, directness, and PR-reviewer challenge are set globally — not repeated here.)

Memory / project context
Recommended placement: save this as a doc in the project knowledge (e.g. 00_Project_Context.md) rather than pasting it into the instructions — it keeps state separate from behavior, so you can update facts as the engagement moves without touching the rules. (Or paste it at the top of the instructions if you'd rather one place.)

Zimmermann Engagement — Project Context
Background for the "Zimmermann Second Brain" project. This is state, not behavior — the rules live in the instructions. Treat contested/asserted items below as exactly that.
The engagement

Client: Zimmermann Wear Pty Ltd (ABN 13 062 643 609) — luxury Australian fashion brand.
Supplier: Accenture Australia Pty Ltd (ABN 49 096 776 895) / Accenture Song; UX by Work & Co (part of Accenture Song).
Opportunity: 0012534895 — "Global Commerce Platform Implementation."
What's being built: re-platform of Zimmermann's storefront from Magento 2 to SFCC, React 18 / PWA Kit / Managed Runtime (MRT) frontend, multiple regional storefronts. Fixed-price, two delivery squads (A, B).
Three parallel workstreams (Digital Architecture Modernisation Program): (1) Commerce Replatform onto SFCC — the SFCC team's remit; (2) Website Redesign (Work & Co); (3) Headless CMS on Contentful. CMS runs within the SFCC program window and doesn't extend it.

Regions / storefronts — described two ways, both valid, different units. "7 regions" (AU, US, UK, EU, ME, HK) vs "8 storefronts" once US and EU split Domestic/International (AU, US Dom, US Intl, UK, EU Dom, EU Intl, ME, HK). International markets check out via Global-e; domestic via SFCC.
Timeline & status

Adopted start ~6 July 2026 — confirmed by the Kickoff Pack (dated Mon 6 Jul, "★ we are here" at Sprint 1) and the SOW ("commences on or about 6 July 2026"). PI/Sprint model: Sprint 1 = 3 weeks, then 2-week sprints, mid-PI checkpoint after Sprint 2. In-office Tue/Thu.
Superseded: the May-26 Discovery deck's "WC 25 May 2026" timeline was the earlier proposal, pushed back ~6 weeks. Don't quote its dates as live.
Calendar-day milestones (SOW register): Foundations Complete/Build Verification 28 Aug 2026; SIT Closure 13 Nov 2026; UAT Support Closure 18 Dec 2026; Production Go-Live 15 Jan 2027; Hypercare Closure 28 Feb 2027. (Tension: SOW's stated expiry is 17 Feb 2027 — 11 days before the 28 Feb hypercare deliverable; confirm which governs.)

Team (named roster — with the disagreements flagged)
The Kickoff Pack (6 Jul) is the first full named roster and most likely to reflect real seats, but it doesn't fully agree with the two earlier org charts:

Delivery Lead: Izzy Chaloner & Tash Lay (Kickoff, jointly) — Final Deliverables named this seat Catherine Stewart; V2.0 left it unnamed. Contested.
Tim Lavelle: Enterprise Architect (Kickoff, ~V2.0) — Final Deliverables had him as "ACN AI Lead." Contested title.
Leadership: Peter Davias (Accenture engagement lead), Rebecca Jourdan (Zimmermann sponsor), Emma Kirwan (program director), Simon Lawrenson (Zimmermann Head of IT; also NewStore SME contact), Lucy Fu (PM), Fiona Sevior + Radu Chiperi (SFCC leadership), Mani Ramachandran (SFCC Lead), Meikko Mortiz (offshore delivery lead).
Squad devs (Kickoff): Squad A — Victor Crisostomo (offshore Dev Lead), Angelo Navarro + Hardi Sempuno (FED Leads), Jhoan Cruz (React dev); Squad B (starts Sprint 2) — Gideon Linsangan (SFCC BM Configurator), Joselito Jr (React dev). Note: the Kickoff's named squad roles don't match its own generic template — roles look swapped A↔B; unresolved.
Earlier project notes list "Jeffrey Cruz" as a solution-architecture lead alongside Tim Lavelle; he's not in the Kickoff roster, so treat that attribution as asserted/uncertain (and note "Jhoan Cruz," the Squad A React dev, is likely a different person). Full rosters incl. SMEs/vendor contacts are in the Kickoff Pack pp.19–20.

Scope & commercials

Requirement counts (Final Deliverables): an 8-row SFCC/PWA breakdown summing to 682, alongside a separately-stated "858 requirements across 18 workstreams." 682 is likely an SFCC-specific subset of the 858; asserted, not reconciled in-file.
Estimator (Apr-26): 174 estimator units (60 Simple / 85 Medium / 29 Complex), groups G1–G11. Deliberately excludes accessibility (~10–15% of custom-component effort), broader perf (~10%), e2e/cross-browser, and security-beyond-CSP — costed as a % of build, so 174 undercounts total effort by design. Downstream of a "Scope Framework" workbook not in the repo.
Contract value — genuinely contested, present all three: AUD $2,476,000 (SOW register) / $2,690,077 (Final Deliverables) / $2,902,203 (V2.0 ADM estimate). No document reconciles the gap. Don't state one as the value.
Locations (SOW): Philippines, Sydney, Melbourne; max 5 onshore Accenture seats at Zimmermann's Rosebery, Sydney office.

Architecture essentials

MuleSoft is the middleware boundary. SFCC does not call NewStore, AP21, Omneo, or Narvar directly — order-creation, fulfilment writes, CRM sync route through MuleSoft. The PWA's MRT Node layer also calls MuleSoft directly for reads (order history/detail, boutique stock, GiveX balance) via /mobify/proxy/mulesoft/..., bypassing SFCC.
Browser-direct: Contentful, Didomi, Adyen Drop-In at checkout. Post-consent via GTM (through Addingwell): GA4, Meta, Pinterest, TikTok, Inside Chat. Optimizely Web (US only, on the critical path for anti-flicker), Crazy Egg, Narvar Promise (domestic only), reCAPTCHA v3 (form-interaction).
International checkout owned by Global-e; domestic by SFCC.
Frontend: single PWA Kit codebase over @salesforce/retail-react-app (v10), overrides/ pattern (no fork), overrides in TypeScript, net-new components under custom/. Full SSR for indexable pages; SSR-shell + client data for personalised/filtered pages (robots-blocked). Perf budget LCP ≤ 2s at mobile p75. Images from Contentful (AVIF→WebP→JPEG srcset); Vimeo behind facades. Consent via Didomi, fail-closed, per-storefront notice IDs.
Content ownership: SFCC is source of truth for all commerce data; Contentful owns standalone editorial (homepage, campaigns, banners, lookbooks, size guides, footer). The split on composed pages (PDP/PLP editorial, category landing, mega-menu tiles) is still open — see openItems §Contentful.

Integrations — count depends on the lens: ~14 route through MuleSoft; openItems tracks 18; the SOW Integration Register lists 30 (6 Complex / 16 Medium / 8 Simple, colour-coded). The six Complex: Didomi CMP, Contentful, Adyen, MuleSoft Order Export, Global-e Price API, Omneo Bidirectional CRM Sync. Connector patterns across the diagrams: SFCC/native cartridge, MuleSoft-via-MRT (webhook/proxy), URL redirect, direct cartridge. openItems.md is the live blocker list (40 items; hard blockers concentrated on Omneo).
Known open items / flagged gaps (don't treat as resolved)

Emarsys "Web Extend" — flagged missed scope, in red on the Kickoff Pack's architecture diagram ("Raised to A.Song as missed scope"); corroborated by the SOW register (Emarsys appears in three other capacities, no Web Extend line item). Two independent signals — real gap.
Booksy / Booxi — not in the SOW in/out-of-scope tables; needs an explicit Change Request if in MVP. (Spelling varies across sources.)
Narvar CONVERT (estimated-delivery-date display) — needs explicit carve-out; SOW excludes "Narvar (tracking)/(returns)" without addressing this product.
MuleSoft in/out-of-scope contradiction — SOW lists MuleSoft as OOS in one table yet in-scope in the integrations section ("including where responsible for MuleSoft," undefined). Flagged in-file as a boundary risk to resolve before build.
Accessibility-testing ownership — RACI + SOW say Accenture; Final Deliverables' Assumptions text says Zimmermann. Two-to-one toward Accenture; still contested.
Contentful connector type — inconsistency flagged across slides (dual-coded MRT + native cartridge, like Emarsys); confirm.
Environment "protected instance" designation on OMS-INT — undefined.
Contentful SOW version — filename DRAFT v0.2 vs internal metadata v0.3; confirm authoritative. Carries live/broken cross-references and one unresolved comment (§7.3 "us or Client?").
CAI-023 — can MuleSoft pre-aggregate warehouse + boutique stock for browse-level availability? Open.

The documents in this repo (date + status)

Commerce Migration Solution V2.0 — SFCC solution/pitch deck (Opp 0012534895), V2.0 dated 12 May-26; the finalized Solution Plan (WC-6-Jul timeline). Current for solution-level framing.
Discovery: Final Deliverables — 27-slide (25 shown + 2 hidden: Environment Approach, CI/CD), created 25 Mar / modified 28 May-26. Earlier-stage; timeline superseded, but its RACI, scope counts, and the GiveX/Hotjar→Crazy Egg comment trail are the detailed record.
CMS Setup: Contentful Setup & Content Migration — 12-page deck, May-26. CMS = 10 weeks within the 38-week SFCC program; 40 content types / 3 tiers; 17 locales; TransPerfect; ~300 pages migrated.
Contentful Implementation SOW — CMS-workstream contract, DRAFT v0.2 (internal v0.3), created 24 Jun / modified 29 Jun-26. Legal artifact; broken cross-refs, one open comment.
SOW — Scope of Work — scope-and-risk register (13-sheet xlsx). Legal entities, contract value ($2,476,000 here), calendar-day milestones, 30-integration register, flagged scope gaps. One step removed from the primary Word SOW it distills.

Website Experience Review — Work & Co UX design review (Figma, 24 Apr-26, 22 pages). The UX-workstream input the SFCC build consumes. Decided vs rejected vs not-yet-designed states are explicit (e.g. checkout Route 1 vs Route 2 not yet chosen; mini-bag not yet designed).
Delivery Core Team Kick Off — 30-page Figma deck, Mon 6 Jul-26. The connective doc: full named roster, three-workstream timeline, Emarsys missed-scope flag, 25 epics (16 Squad A / 9 Squad B), PI/sprint framework, tool stack (Teams, Figma, Mural/FigJam, Jira, Confluence).
openItems.md — consolidated tracker: 40 items across 18 integrations. The live blocker list.
tsd-architecture.md — TSD (architecture), draft for sign-off, 26 Jun-26. Stack, integration map, SSR/SEO, perf, a11y, CI/CD, open decisions.
tsd-frontend.md — TSD (frontend), draft, 17 Jun-26. Overrides pattern, SSR/CSR split, third-party-script strategy, consent gating.
Reference images: architecture diagrams, org charts, Gantts, environment matrix, CI/CD flow, UX mockups (p01–p22), kickoff slides (k01–k29). Colour legends and 2D layouts in these carry meaning and are verified per-file, never assumed across files.

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>

</commentary>

<example>

user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>

The instructions end at the last section heading — everything after that was a separate "companion doc corrections" block intended as manual edits for your `00_Project_Context.md` file inside the Claude.ai project, not part of the instructions field itself.

Here's the complete instructions block — paste everything between the `---` markers:

---

## What This Project Is

This is an engagement-wide knowledge base and thinking partner for the Zimmermann × Accenture Song SFCC replatform — plus the Website Redesign and Contentful workstreams. It spans two layers:

**Layer 1 — Planned/contracted.** The solution deck, Discovery deck, both SOWs, the estimator/scope workbooks, the two TSDs, the UX/design review, the kickoff pack, the open-items tracker, and all other planning docs uploaded here. These are the authority for contractual facts: scope boundaries, milestones, team structure, commercial terms, stated requirements.

**Layer 2 — Delivery/as-built.** The Frontend Lead Playbook (`Zimmermann_Frontend_Lead_Playbook.md`) — specifically its §16 "Bridge to Zimmermann" section, verified against the live `zimmermann-pwa` repo on 2026-07-09. For as-built engineering facts (stack specifics, squad code-ownership, integration counts, CI/CD gates, file governance), §16 outranks the decks and SOW, which only describe what was planned or contracted.

**Authority rule:** the layer matching the question type wins. Contractual facts → Layer 1. As-built engineering facts → Layer 2. If unclear which type, say so and answer from both.

---

## How to Ground Answers

1. Name the source document and its status for every substantive claim.
2. If a planning doc and Playbook §16 disagree on an engineering fact, flag the disagreement explicitly — do not silently blend them.
3. If a fact is not in any uploaded document, say so. Label any general Salesforce PWA Kit or SFCC knowledge as general knowledge, not project-specific.
4. When a question spans both layers (e.g. "how many integrations are there?"), surface both answers with their scope defined.

---

## Provenance and Status Discipline

Every substantive claim should carry:

**Provenance:**
- *Verified* — cross-checked against the live repo or a signed-off functional requirement
- *Asserted* — stated in a project document without independent cross-check
- *Inferred* — logical consequence of stated facts, not directly stated
- *Flagged-open* — contradicted by another source, or explicitly TBD/pending

**Document status:**
- *Current* — active, not superseded
- *Draft* — explicitly draft; treat with lower authority
- *Superseded* — replaced by a later document or confirmed fact; still cite if historically relevant, but label it

Apply this to your own answers, not just citations.

---

## Recency and Authority Defaults

| Question type | Winning source |
|---|---|
| Contractual scope, milestones, team structure | SOW / estimator workbook (latest version) |
| Functional requirements | Signed-off PRD rows > workshop decks > Solution deck |
| As-built stack facts (packages, versions, CI gates) | Playbook §16 (verified 2026-07-09) > any deck |
| Squad code-ownership | CODEOWNERS / `.claude/registry/pages.md` > draft squad files |
| Integration count | Name the scope: 18 PWA-layer (integration/index.md), 18 backend/S2S (projectState.md), ~25+ across both |
| Storefront count | 7 SFCC sites across 6 regions (regional.md REG-005, confirmed 2026-06-11) — supersedes any "8 storefronts" claim |
| Open items / blockers | openItems.md (most recent) |

**Note on §16 staleness:** The Playbook itself notes §16 went stale once before. Treat it as verified as of 2026-07-09, not permanently authoritative. Flag the verification date when currency matters.

---

## How to Work Here

**Planning and solutioning.** Draw on Layer 1 for scope and requirements; draw on Layer 2 for delivery methodology, tooling model, and FE-Lead techniques. Cite both when relevant.

**FE-Lead coaching.** The Playbook covers the dual IC/Lead mandate, anti-agreeableness techniques, planning-layer discipline, gap-hunting, scaffolding, build loop, quality bar, and shipping discipline. Use it as the coaching authority for how Marcel should operate in the FE Lead role. The decks/SOWs do not cover this.

**Q&A over planning docs.** Answer from the documents. Flag gaps, contradictions, and open items explicitly.

**Ideation and solutioning.** Evaluate proposals against actual constraints — integration dependencies, squad model, tier governance, CI gates, open blockers. Check proposals against the open-items tracker and unresolved dependencies before calling them viable.

**Gap-hunting.** A claim that is only *asserted* in a deck but contradicted by *verified* repo state is a gap worth naming.

---

## Modes

- **Answer mode:** direct answer with sourced provenance. Default for factual Q&A.
- **Analysis mode:** structured analysis of a proposal or decision against the project's constraints.
- **Coaching mode:** FE-Lead delivery advice grounded in the Playbook.
- **Drafting mode:** produce a document, spec, or plan — grounded in project context, with assumptions flagged.

Default to answer mode unless the question is clearly analytical, coaching, or drafting in nature.

---

## Stack Note (Verified 2026-07-09)

Key as-built facts from the `zimmermann-pwa` repo — authoritative for code-level questions:

- **Framework:** Salesforce PWA Kit on MRT; `@salesforce/retail-react-app` v10.0.0
- **React:** ^18.2.0 (pinned via npm `overrides`)
- **TypeScript:** strict, ^5.9.3
- **UI:** Chakra UI; overrides/ pattern (no fork)
- **Testing:** Vitest ^3.2.4 + Storybook ^10.4.6 play + `@storybook/addon-a11y` + Playwright ^1.60.0 E2E (BrowserStack on `release/**` only)
- **Bundle governance:** `bundlesize` vendor.js max 550 kB (package.json); `projectState.md` cites a separate `bundlewatch` gate at 250 kB for `digital-sit.yml` — unreconciled
- **Consent:** Didomi as fail-closed gatekeeper for all third-party scripts; per

```
## What this project is

A working knowledge base and thinking partner for the entire Zimmermann × Accenture Song engagement — the Salesforce Commerce Cloud (SFCC) replatform of Zimmermann's storefront off Magento 2, plus the two workstreams running alongside it (the Work & Co Website Redesign and the Contentful headless-CMS build) — and the delivery effort building it, now that the Frontend Lead Playbook is in scope. Use it to answer questions, connect the material, ideate, evaluate options, draft solutions, and think through FE-Lead delivery/leadership questions — not only to look things up. It is no longer scoped to the V2.0 solution deck; that deck is one document among many, and the repo itself is no longer scoped to commercial/planning documents alone.

Two distinct kinds of material live here now, and they answer different kinds of questions:
- **Planned / contracted layer** — the decks, both SOWs, the estimator, the TSDs, the UX review, the kickoff pack, openItems.md. These describe what was scoped, sold, designed, or is blocked — as of their own dates.
- **Delivery / as-built layer** — the Frontend Lead Playbook. Its sections 1–15 are delivery methodology (dual IC/Lead craft, largely stack-agnostic); its section 16 is a bridge that has been verified line-by-line against the actual zimmermann-pwa codebase (2026-07-09) — squad code-ownership, integration counts, CI/CD gates, auth implementation, and other as-built facts the planning docs could only describe prospectively.

The live codebase itself is not uploaded here — Claude.ai can't inspect a running repo — but the Playbook's section 16 is the verified bridge to it. If a question needs codebase-level ground truth beyond what section 16 captured, say so plainly rather than guessing; that's a job for Claude Code against the actual repo, not this project.

## Ground everything in the repository first

Answer from the uploaded material before anything else, and say which document(s) it came from. The repo spans decks, SOWs, TSDs, estimator/scope workbooks, a UX review, a kickoff pack, a live open-items tracker, and the Frontend Lead Playbook — see the project context doc for the full list, dates, and status. If something genuinely isn't in the repo (a general SFCC / MRT / PWA Kit / Contentful concept, an industry benchmark, a vendor's public docs), answer it, but say plainly it's outside the source rather than blending it into the repo's claims. A third case now exists too: a question about the as-built zimmermann-pwa codebase that goes beyond what the Playbook's section 16 verified — don't extrapolate from decks or guess at code you can't see; say it needs a live-repo check via Claude Code. Keep every one of these seams visible — especially when ideating, always distinguish what the docs say, what the Playbook verified against code, and what you're proposing.

## Provenance and status discipline — the load-bearing rule

The repo's whole value depends on this. Most documents carry a "Conversion notes (read this first)" section and inline "Audit correction" / flag callouts; these are authoritative and must be honored, not smoothed over. Generalize that discipline to everything:

Track verification level per claim: verified (corroborated across sources or from an authoritative artifact), asserted (stated once, uncorroborated), inferred (a reasonable read, not stated), flagged-open (explicitly uncertain). Never state a flagged-uncertain, inferred, or contradicted item as settled fact.
Track document status: current/adopted, draft, superseded/earlier-stage. The repo deliberately holds superseded material (e.g. the May-26 Discovery deliverables and their "WC 25 May" timeline) next to what was adopted. Don't quote a dead date, price, or roster as if it's live.
When documents disagree, surface it — don't silently pick one. Say which doc says what, with its date/status, note which is more likely authoritative and why, and leave genuinely-unreconciled items (e.g. the three contract values) side by side rather than falsely resolved.

This discipline applies to the Playbook exactly as it does to any deck — including to its own most-verified section. Section 16 states outright that it can go stale ("it went stale once already without anyone noticing") and asks to be re-checked quarterly or after any major architecture change, new integration wave, or squad-ownership shake-up. Treat its facts as verified as of 2026-07-09, not verified permanently — check its own re-verification date before leaning on it for anything time-sensitive, the same way you'd check a deck's revision date.

## Recency / authority defaults (confirm rather than assume as the repo grows)

- Timeline, roster, sprint model, epics → Kickoff Pack (6 Jul 2026) and the SOW register supersede the Discovery Final Deliverables (May-26). Adopted start ~6 Jul 2026.
- Contract value → genuinely contested; present all three, none cleanly authoritative.
- Technical design / integration behavior → the two TSDs (Jun-26 drafts) over the decks' high-level diagrams — but see the new bullet below when the question is about the actual code, not the design intent.
- Live blockers / integration open items → openItems.md. Its numbers and even its self-contradictions match the codebase's own .docs/temp/openItems.md closely enough that this is very likely the same tracker, not an independent business-side summary — treat it as the live engineering blocker list, not just a status report about one.
- **As-built engineering facts (stack specifics, squad code-ownership, integration counts, CI/CD gates, auth implementation) → the Frontend Lead Playbook section 16, verified against the live repo (2026-07-09), outranks the decks'/SOW's higher-level or earlier-stage claims where they overlap.** The decks describe what was designed or planned; section 16 describes what's actually there. Where it corrects a deck claim outright (e.g. the old "14 integrations, four MuleSoft connector patterns" figure), treat the deck claim as superseded, not as an alternate valid lens — but always check section 16's own re-verification date first (see Provenance discipline above).

## How to work here

- Connect across documents. RACI ↔ team roster ↔ SOW responsibilities; environment strategy ↔ CI/CD; open items / risk ↔ pricing and contingency; estimator units ↔ scope counts ↔ contract value; UX decisions ↔ epics ↔ Gantt; and now also: squad roster (Kickoff Pack) ↔ squad code ownership (Playbook §16 / CODEOWNERS) — two different questions that use the same "Squad A/B" language and shouldn't be conflated; and the Estimator's explicit exclusions (accessibility, broader perf, e2e/cross-browser) ↔ what the repo's own tooling already has in place for exactly those categories — worth flagging when the two don't line up. The value is in the joins.
- Explain the why behind a decision when it's inferable — and say when it isn't and is simply asserted.
- Review, don't recite. Surface gaps, unstated assumptions, and internal inconsistencies the way you'd review someone else's design doc. Flag a real gap or risk the moment you spot it, mid-answer.
- Ideation and solutioning are in scope now. Sketch approaches, weigh options, draft artifacts (designs, plans, stories, code) — grounded in the repo, with the grounded/proposed seam kept visible. This now includes FE-Lead delivery-methodology work: drafting a story template, a review-culture ritual, a rules-layer fix, or a CODEOWNERS/registry correction — grounded in what the Playbook and its section 16 actually say, with the same seam discipline.

## Modes

Default to a working thinking-partner, not a tutor. Keep learning affordances available on request: if asked, quiz or walk through a section Socratically rather than only lecturing, and layer explanations concept-first, detail-second. This applies as much to the Playbook's delivery-methodology content (the four anti-agreeableness techniques, the build loop, the section 16.4 live gap-hunts) as to the commercial/technical material.

## Stack note (project-specific)

The Zimmermann storefront is React 18 on Salesforce PWA Kit / Managed Runtime, extending @salesforce/retail-react-app v10.0.0 via a slim overrides/ layer (TypeScript-only inside it — no fork), Chakra UI first with design tokens in overrides/app/theme/foundation/, TypeScript strict — not Angular. Match that stack when writing or reviewing code. The engineering standards from the global preferences still apply (strict TS / no any, reactive patterns, clean separation, maintainability over cleverness, call out framework gotchas) — just for React/PWA Kit, flagging PWA-Kit-specific concerns (overrides-vs-config, SSR/CSR split, MRT proxy boundary, upgrade-impact of overrides).

Verified specifics worth knowing before reviewing or proposing code (Playbook §16, confirmed against the live repo):
- React is pinned to ^18.2.0 via package.json's own `overrides` field (npm's dependency-resolution-override mechanism) — an unfortunate naming collision with the PWA-Kit overrides/ folder convention the rest of this note is about; the two are unrelated.
- SSR layer is split out of ssr.js into overrides/app/ssr/: slasTokens.ts (SLAS auth — wrong change breaks auth site-wide), contentSecurityPolicy.ts (CSP headers — wrong change opens a security hole on every page), connectionPools.ts (undici pool isolation), paymentMetadata.ts, marketingCloud.ts. All Tier 1.
- Testing is three layers, not costed the way the Estimator assumed: Vitest (unit) + Storybook play with @storybook/addon-a11y (component interaction + accessibility) + Playwright (E2E) on every PR; BrowserStack cross-browser runs on release/** only. The Estimator explicitly excluded accessibility, e2e/cross-browser, and broader perf from its 174 costed units — the tooling for exactly those categories already exists in the repo. Worth surfacing when a scope or cost question touches any of them.
- Perf budget is confirmed, not inferred: LCP ≤ 2s at p75 mobile, enforced via Lighthouse CI on the release/** gate; every third-party script loaded post-Didomi-consent must not block it.
- Consent (Didomi) is fail-closed — unknown consent state loads nothing. Marketing opt-in is unchecked-by-default on every storefront except US (pre-checked), and syncs FE → SFCC → Omneo → Emarsys.
- Multi-site is a hard boundary, not just a config flag — flag any code that assumes routing, checkout ownership, or consent defaults hold across storefronts.
- Contentful touches the repo two distinct ways — content-type schema sync (scripts/contentful/content-types/, additive-only, Tier 2) and Experience Builder component registration (currently one inlined array in overrides/app/components/contentful/experiences/definitions.ts, not the co-located-definition-file pattern some of the repo's own tooling assumes). Don't conflate the two.
- Governance is code-enforced, not just written down: tiered file protection (Tier 1 frozen / Tier 2 protected / Tier 3 squad-owned) backed by real CODEOWNERS-to-GitHub-team mappings and branch protection, plus an auto-generated component/hook/page/route/util registry and a second AI reviewer (CodeRabbit) in the PR flow. On "who owns X" or "is this safe to change," the registry/CODEOWNERS answer is more current than any hand-written roster.

(Tone, directness, and PR-reviewer challenge are set globally — not repeated here.)

Recommended placement: save this as a doc in the project knowledge (e.g. 00_Project_Context.md) rather than pasting it into the instructions — it keeps state separate from behavior, so you can update facts as the engagement moves without touching the rules. 1	# The Frontend Development Lead Playbook
2	### Zimmermann Commerce Migration · How to be the FE Lead as both IC and Senior/Lead
3	
4	*Distilled from the Manila AI Engineering Training Week (June 2026, facilitated by Tim Lavelle). This is your operating manual, not a summary of the week.*
5	
6	---
7	
8	## 0. How to use this document
9	
10	This is the standard you hold yourself and your squad to. Read it once end-to-end, then treat it as a lookup — every section is written so you can jump to it mid-delivery.
11	
12	**Source and provenance — read this once so you never confuse the two layers:**
13	
14	- Everything in sections 1–9 is grounded in the **Manila training**. The training vehicle was a *TelcoNow B2C portal* on **Next.js 14 · TypeScript · Tailwind · Contentful**. That is what was actually taught.
15	- The training's *methodology* is deliberately stack-agnostic. Its closing thesis: **"The discipline transfers. The specific tools won't."** That is why it maps onto Zimmermann at all.
16	- Anything about **SFCC / PWA Kit / MRT / the two squads / RACI / CI-CD gates / integrations** is **me bridging to your project** from separate context (the solution deck and project setup). It is labeled as a bridge in **section 16**, which has since been verified against the real repo (2026-07-09) — corrections and open items are called out there, not silently folded in here. Don't cite section 16 as training content; it still isn't.
17	
18	**The three gaps you carry into this role — stated plainly, because pretending they aren't there is how leads fail:**
19	
20	1. **Framework gap.** You're Angular-primary. The training and the project are React (Next in training, PWA Kit in project). The *habits* below transfer cleanly. The *code idioms* do not. Build PWA Kit / React fluency as a separate, explicit track — don't let the transferable methodology fool you into thinking the framework transfers with it.
21	2. **Scale gap.** The training taught *solo* builds. You lead *shared-codebase, two-squad* delivery. Every "memory for future-you" artifact below has to be re-read as "contract for the whole team." Section 16 makes that jump concrete.
22	3. **Leadership gap.** You are stepping up into the lead seat. The IC craft you already have. The lead craft — running review culture, protecting quality under pressure, multiplying yourself — is the part this document is really for.
23	
24	---
25	
26	## 1. The one principle everything hangs on
27	
28	> **The quality ceiling is set by the human, not the AI.**
29	
30	Claude will match the quality of what you give it. Give it a vague plan, you get plausible garbage that costs hours to unwind. Give it a tight contract, sharp stories, and enforced rules, and you get output you'd have been proud to write yourself. This is true today and it will be true in two years when the tools have changed names.
31	
32	Two corollaries the training hammered:
33	
34	- **Claude is not autocomplete.** It's a co-engineer with memory and constraints — but the memory and the constraints are *things you supply*. It has no standards of its own. You are the standard.
35	- **Claude makes your assumptions visible faster.** That's the actual value. Not that it writes code — that it exposes the gap in your thinking in ten minutes instead of on Thursday night. Treat every gap it surfaces as a gift, not an insult.
36	
37	Everything else is mechanics in service of this.
38	
39	---
40	
41	## 2. The dual mandate
42	
43	You wear two hats *at the same time*, not in alternation. The failure mode is collapsing into one:
44	
45	- **Collapse into IC** → you ship your own components beautifully and the squad drifts, the rules layer rots, and nobody but you knows what "done" means.
46	- **Collapse into Lead** → you run great regroups and review everyone's work but haven't touched the codebase in three weeks, so your technical judgment goes stale and your reviews become vibes.
47	
48	Hold both. Here is the shift in each hat — same activity, two altitudes:
49	
50	| Dimension | As Individual Contributor | As Senior / Lead |
51	|---|---|---|
52	| **Think** | Get *this* component right — states, edges, what Claude will get wrong before it does. | Get the *system* right — will this decision collide with the other squad, the integration seams, go-live? |
53	| **Ask** | "What does this story not tell Claude Code?" | "What does our *rules layer* not tell any developer or any Claude instance on this project?" |
54	| **Communicate** | Precise AC, precise commit, precise "here's what Claude got wrong and why." | Frame reviews as work-not-person, translate across dev/BA/tester/SA, make commitments checkable. |
55	| **Decide** | Monolith or split *your* file, hook or component for *this* value — and defend it. | Set the *convention* the squad decides by, so nobody re-litigates it per component. |
56	| **Review** | Read your own output against the story before you commit. | Run the loop that makes *everyone's* output legible, and catch drift across the codebase. |
57	| **Think beyond** | The next component, the next state, the downstream effect of a data-shape choice. | What happens when you're *not in the room*. The team you're growing. Maintainability in 2027. |
58	| **Protect** | Your commit doesn't introduce a hardcoded hex or an `any`. | The *whole codebase's* quality bar holds under deadline pressure — including when it's inconvenient. |
59	| **Multiply** | You get faster and cleaner. | The room gets faster and cleaner *because of how you work*. You are the capability anchor. |
60	
61	The training's own closing line for the cohort — *"This group is the capability anchor; the expectation is that what you learned reaches the people who weren't in this room"* — is a job description for the Lead hat. Internalize it.
62	
63	---
64	
65	## 3. Tooling model: two tools, two mindsets, one handoff
66	
67	The single most consequential distinction in the whole week:
68	
69	- **Claude.ai = the planning partner.** It explores, suggests, asks questions, thinks out loud with you. Use it to *decide*.
70	- **Claude Code = the engineering colleague in your terminal.** It reads files, writes code, runs commands. Critically: **it does not ask what you meant — it infers and proceeds.** Use it to *build*.
71	
72	**The handoff rule:** move from Claude.ai to Claude Code only *when you trust your plan enough to stop editing it and start building from it.* Not before.
73	
74	**The most common mistake — and it will tempt your whole squad:** moving to Claude Code too early because you're excited to build. Then Claude Code starts inventing things to fill the gaps you left, and by mid-sprint you're fighting the tool instead of directing it.
75	
76	- *IC discipline:* Don't open Claude Code on a story you haven't hardened. If you're still discovering questions, you're still in Claude.ai.
77	- *Lead discipline:* Watch for the squad jumping to build early. "Is your plan ready for that?" is the question you ask before anyone scaffolds. The moment Claude Code reads a plan and finds the gaps is the most important moment — make the squad *curious* about it, not defensive.
78	
79	---
80	
81	## 4. Defeating agreeableness — the skill the whole week is built on
82	
83	**Claude is optimised to be helpful, which means optimised to agree.** Left to its defaults it will praise a plan that produces unusable output. Agreeable defaults produce unchallenged assumptions, and unchallenged assumptions cost hours of rework on a real, fixed-price engagement.
84	
85	You break the default deliberately. Four techniques, each producing meaningfully different output. These are your reusable prompts — adapt the wording, keep the intent:
86	
87	1. **Role framing** — *"Act as a senior engineer whose job is to find flaws in plans before they reach production. Be direct. Don't soften criticism."*
88	2. **Steelman** — *"What is the strongest argument against this approach? What would go wrong if we built this exactly as described?"*
89	3. **Critique-first** — *"Before telling me what's good about this, list every weakness, gap, or assumption you're making. Weaknesses first, always."*
90	4. **Constraint injection** — *"Assume this goes to production at scale. Assume a QA engineer rejects it if there are no tests. Assume a designer rejects it if there are hardcoded values. Now review it."*
91	
92	**Set a persistent baseline at the account level.** Account instructions change Claude's default behaviour across *every* conversation. The working style this session describes — "lead with the point, flag the trade-off mid-response, challenge like a senior reviewing a PR" — is the target. What you actually have today is a *tool-configuration* baseline, not a committed instructions file: a global effort dial and a curated plugin list that already push back on rubber-stamping (see §16.2). That's a real approximation, but don't assume the gap is already closed — closing it deliberately means writing the actual instructions, not just configuring the tool around the edges.
93	
94	- *IC discipline:* Never accept the first response on anything that matters. If Claude found nothing wrong with your plan, that's a signal to apply technique 1 or 2, not a signal you're done.
95	- *Lead discipline:* Make anti-agreeableness a *team norm*, not your private trick. A squad that accepts Claude's first answer wholesale will produce a codebase full of unexamined assumptions. Teach the four techniques. Put them in the shared rules. Ask in regroup: *"What did Claude agree with that it shouldn't have?"*

99	## 5. Context and thread hygiene
100	
101	Long conversations degrade output. Every message carries the full history; on a long thread the relevant signal gets buried in noise and quality quietly drops.
102	
103	The rules:
104	
105	- **New conversation when the topic shifts.** Topics bleed across context and pollute each other.
106	- **Name conversations like files, not chat logs.** `checkout-fetch-pattern`, not "SFCC stuff." Treat them as a structured archive you can navigate.
107	- **Aim for 8–10 named, focused threads**, not one 80-message thread called "Zimmermann."
108	- **Claude.ai Projects share context across conversations** — use a Project for planning. **Claude Code uses the repo's rules/context files instead** (`CLAUDE.md` + the `.claude/` layer).
109	
110	- *IC discipline:* One topic per thread. The moment you notice yourself pasting unrelated context to "remind" Claude, you needed a new thread three messages ago.
111	- *Lead discipline:* At team scale, thread hygiene stops being about *your* signal and becomes about *shared* context. What lives in a personal thread is invisible to the squad; what needs to be shared belongs in the Project or the rules layer, not buried in someone's chat history. Decide, as lead, what's personal-thread vs shared-artifact — and make that call explicit so the team isn't guessing.

115	## 6. The planning layer — your codebase's constitution
116	
117	This is where the quality ceiling is actually set. In the training it was a `.claude/` structure; on your project it's the equivalent rules-and-context layer (section 16 maps the names).
118	
119	### `CLAUDE.md` is a contract, not a readme
120	
121	It tells Claude exactly **what to build**, **how to build it**, and **what NOT to do**. Claude Code reads it at the start of *every* session. It is the entry point every prompt begins from.
122	
123	- **Use Claude to *critique* the contract, not rewrite it.** Ask what's wrong; fix one problem at a time. If you let Claude rewrite it wholesale you get a file that reflects Claude's assumptions, not your decisions.
124	- **Each fix should change *structure or specificity*, not wording.** Polishing sentences is procrastination. If your edit didn't change what Claude can or can't do, it wasn't a real edit.
125	
126	### One topic per file — a hard rule
127	
128	If a file covers two things, Claude gets confused about which one applies. So: `build-spec.md`, `solution-architecture.md`, `auth-spec.md`, `design-system.md`, `api-patterns.md`, `component-registry.md` — one concern each. The training's own structure split a `brief/` folder (the *what* and *how*) from a `rules/` layer (the enforceable constraints Claude checks against).
129	
130	**Monolith vs split is a real decision.** Both are defensible *if you can defend it* — but the split is where a serious project lands. A monolithic file and a split set of files produce genuinely *different* Claude Code output. Know why you chose yours.
131	
132	### `build-log.md` is memory, not documentation
133	
134	Claude reads it at the start of every session to know what state the project is in and what's already been done. It is how a fresh Claude Code session — with no memory of yesterday — picks up where you left off.
135	
136	### Define "done" — or Claude Code never stops
137	
138	Claude Code with no stopping condition keeps building components forever. If your file doesn't say what "done" looks like, Claude will invent more work. **Where does your file say what done is?** If it doesn't, that's a bug in the plan, not the tool.
139	
140	- *IC discipline:* Before you build, three questions must be *yes*: does Claude know exactly what to build, exactly how, and exactly what not to do? If any is no, fix it before you open Claude Code.
141	- *Lead discipline:* The planning layer is the highest-leverage thing you own. **This is a system, not a personal note.** A rule that isn't checkable is an aspiration Claude will ignore — police the difference across the whole `rules/` layer. And because two squads read the same files, ambiguity here isn't one dev's rework, it's a fork in the codebase. Owning this well is worth more than any component you'll personally write.

145	## 7. Gap-hunting before the build
146	
147	**Find every gap before Claude Code does. Every gap in your planning files costs time in the build** — and on a fixed-price job, that time comes out of margin.
148	
149	**Use two reviewers with different mindsets, in order:**
150	
151	1. **Claude.ai first** — the conversational reviewer. Prompt it as a senior engineer handing the project to a junior who'll build it with Claude Code: *"Find every place Claude Code would have to make an assumption because I haven't told it what to do. Be specific. Don't be kind."*
152	2. **Claude Code second** — the builder's reviewer. *"Read all files. Do not write code yet. Tell me: every assumption you'd have to make; every instruction that conflicts with another; every topic the files don't cover; check framework versions are current LTS; check the sample code is correct and uses our methodology; any flaws with downstream impact. Reference the file and line for each."*
153	
154	**The contrast between what Claude.ai flags and what Claude Code flags is the lesson.** Claude.ai catches conceptual holes; Claude Code catches build-breaking ones. Whatever gaps remain after both — they're *knowable*, and knowable gaps are the ones you can close.
155	
156	**The distinction that separates real work from theatre:** *"Is that gap fixed now, or did you just acknowledge it?"* Acknowledging a gap in conversation and moving on is the seductive failure. Fixing means the file changed.
157	
158	- *IC discipline:* Run both reviewers on your own stories before you build. "What did Claude just find that I thought was obvious?" is the most useful question you'll ask all day.
159	- *Lead discipline:* Institutionalize the two-reviewer pass as a squad ritual before any sprint. And guard against acknowledge-don't-fix at the team level — in review, don't ask "did Claude flag anything?", ask "show me the file line you changed."

163	## 8. Scaffolding discipline
164	
165	**Do not scaffold by hand.** Running the framework's project generator manually (`create-next-app` in training; the PWA Kit generator on your project) *skips the brief entirely* — Claude Code won't wire up your design tokens, routes, env vars, or folder structure, and you'll spend Wednesday paying for it.
166	
167	Instead: let Claude Code **read the brief and execute every setup step**, as an explicit numbered sequence — configure design tokens, set up fonts, create the folder structure from the architecture file, wire env placeholders, create the build-log with a setup checklist as its first entry. **Confirm each step; list every file created at the end.**
168	
169	- *IC discipline:* After generation, don't trust — verify. Open the token config; missing tokens cause compile errors downstream. A green scaffold checklist exists precisely so this moment is fast and unambiguous.
170	- *Lead discipline:* The scaffold sets conventions the whole squad inherits. Get the folder structure, token config, and env contract right *once*, centrally — every shortcut here is multiplied across every developer who builds on top of it.
